subtopic: ADEQUACY OF LABOUR FORCE DURING SHIPPING SEASON

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ADEQUACY OF LABOUR FORCE DURING SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the fear expressed in British shipping circles, can the minister assure the house that an adequate labour force will be on hand at the port of Churchill during the shipping season to handle grain and goods to the full capacity of the port?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ADEQUACY OF LABOUR FORCE DURING SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's question
was directed to me just a short while ago. While I have not a full report, I think I have sufficient information to answer the question. He asks whether there will be sufficient labour at the port of Churchill to look after shipments of grain and goods to the United Kingdom. I must say to him first of all that it is not the responsibility of the national harbours board to look after stevedoring operations. That is the responsibility of the shipping firms and their agents. But in the past the national harbours board has followed the practice of recruiting a labour force in that area. It is willing to do that. I am informed by the port manager that some sixty-five or seventy men will be required to do that work, and we think it will be possible to get that force.
The hon. gentleman in his question goes on to ask if grain and goods to the full
capacity of the port can be handed by the
labour force. I must say to him that if his question is directed to mixed cargoes of grain and lumber, I do not think there will be a great deal of difficulty. If it is directed to lumber alone, then it will take an additional one hundred men, and I do not think it will be possible to recruit that force. However, the national harbours board will do its utmost to assist if notified of the labour force required. It has all facilities available at Churchill for general cargo. I wanted the hon. gentleman to keep in mind the fact that the responsibility for stevedoring is not that of the board but rather that of the shipping companies.

subtopic: ADEQUACY OF LABOUR FORCE DURING SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext:
If there is any question as
to the port of Churchill being able to handle these shipments, I suggest they be handled through the port of Halifax.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.

National health branch-
215.	Assistance to provinces for control of venereal diseases under regulations approved by the governor in council, $175,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister give the expenditure under this item? I should like to have the breakdown of grants by provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Estimate for 1946-47, $175,000; expenditure for the same period, $171,850.29; unliquidated commitments, $1,242.05.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This item provides for assistance to the provinces for the control of venereal diseases under regulations approved by the governor in council. If the same basis of distribution is .in effect as was in effect during the previous year, the division is based, thirty per cent on the population, forty per cent on the extent of the venereal disease problem, and thirty per cent on the financial needs of the province. Will the minister give the distribution of the money to the provinces, please?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The net cash grants were as follows:
Prince Edward Island	 $ 4,297.94
Nova Scotia	 9,462.28
New Brunswick	 7,968.86
Quebec	 38,165.64
Ontario	 42,494 .'11
Manitoba	 10,585.88
Saskatchewan	 11,649.23
Alberta	  11,463.74

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The balance, I take it, represents that educational reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And if I understand correctly that work of education, for which the sum of approximately $25,000 was reserved, is carried on directly under the federal Department of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I think it is appreciated by all hon. members that this work in combating venereal disease is largely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and that apart from extraordinary times such as existed during the war, wyhen the federal government had an opportunity to render more active assistance in this field, in normal times the field open to the federal government is somewhat limited. But I would like to ask the minister whether, apart from making these grants out of this sum of $175,000 a year, the federal government is doing anything to encourage or assist the provinces in developing more active measures for discovering the sources and extent of venereal disease. The minister is aware, as I hope the entire committee is aware, of an important step taken in recent months in Ontario, for instance, in connection with prenatal tests. I think it is of interest to the house to learn the results of those tests. This information was given to the press by the Ontario department of health, and appeared in various newspapers on May 15 of this year. The newspaper article states:
An average of 3,900 expectant mothers per month have been taking advantage of the Ontario health department's offer of one free prenatal examination by their own physician, it is shown in figures released at Queen's Park yesterday.
While the act authorizing this examination at the expense of the province was passed at the 1946 session, it did not become operative until October 1 last. Since that time and up until April 30 last, 27,332 women in 346 municipalities have been examined on this basis by 1,243 physicians. The province pays $5 for each examination upon which a report is submitted.
Department officials said "screening" of the reports to extract significant data from them is proceeding slowly and it is too early to comment upon this phase of the work. The incidence of "V.D." however, is below that anticipated.
I should like to add this observation, that of course the compilation of information as to the incidence of venereal disease is only one of the purposes of the free prenatal test; but having regard to .the results already obtained I do suggest to the minister that if anything can be done within the proper scope and function of his department to encourage other provinces to undertake the provision of

free prenatal tests, the advantages accruing not only in connection with combating venereal disease but in connection with combating other very serious inroads on the public health of the nation will be very greatly increased.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister one question in regard to this item. I have not been paying strict attention, and he may have replied to it already. What supervision does the federal department have in connection with this grant of $175,000 to see that it is properly used for the purpose for which it is made?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman will understand, this is primarily a function of the provinces, but we do help through the distribution of funds, the collection and compilation and analysis of statistical data concerning venereal infection, through the preparation of lay and professional educational material using all appropriate media, and through the provision of consultative professional medical services. We do try to encourage any provinces which may not seem to have done as much as others, by way of suggestions. At annual meetings of the dominion council of health, where all the provincial governments are represented through their deputy ministers, we have an opportunity of bringing to their attention what has been done in particular provinces where advances have been outstanding. The hon. member for Eglinton has just referred to something which is done in one specific province. At the last meeting of the council, about four weeks ago, the representative of Ontario indicated to the others what they had done. This kind of exchange of information is carried on. Then at the end of the fiscal year each provincial government submits a detailed statement of the expenditure of federal funds and the purposes for which those funds were used, including a detailed narrative report indicating the actual accomplishments of the venereal disease control programme in that province, accompanied by substantiating statistical information. Every effort is made to meet this problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am aware that this problem falls within provincial jurisdiction and that the federal department helps out. All I had in mind-and I think the minister has satisfactorily answered my question-is that if any province did not make proper use of the grants, in my opinion the grants should not be continued to that province. That was the purpose of my question.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The grant would not be continued in such case, but I am happy to say there has been no such instance as yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am happy to hear it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I want to ask the minister a question regarding the statement made last night by Doctor W. E. Gallie, dean of medicine of the university of Toronto, concerning the rural portions of the country outside the cities and towns. At a dinner given in his honour last night-he has been chief surgeon of the Toronto General Hospital for many years-he proposed that zones should be mapped out all over Canada for specialists in surgery, so they could have all the facilities which modern science and medicine have produced in recent years, particularly during the war. My question to the minister follows closely along the lines of what I had to say the other evening in reference to greater medical aid to these universities throughout our land that are doing such great work. After all is said and done, medical science has played a tremendous part in the life of the country, and important discoveries have been made in recent years. We are now on the verge of a great revolution in medicine and surgery; and in order that people in remote places may have the full benefit of scientific developments I believe the government would be well advised, by bonuses, subventions and subsidies, to support the type of federal aid suggested by Doctor Gallie, which people do not now receive. We know that patriotic citizens have helped hospitals, and that they have helped medical science and dental science but, owing to the heavy taxation they cannot carry the whole burden. I wish the minister would study this matter and confer with the authorities of the university of Toronto and other universities, to see if federal aid along the lines I have indicated cannot be provided. Perhaps the minister would make a statement in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member, who is keenly interested in this matter, has spoken to me privately about it on several occasions. I believe he has spoken also to my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply under whose department the national research council operates. I too have been interested in this problem, and I may say to him that the matter to which he has referred is under active consideration.
As the hon. member knows, one of the eminent scientists of Ontario, Doctor C. H. Best, who by the way is a great friend of the hon. member, is one of the members of the medical research division of the national research council. Doctor Collip, Doctor Simard and several other distinguished scientists also serve on the committee which keeps this problem under constant review. While I am not in a position to make any further statement with regard to future prospects, I can say that the question raised by the hon. member is one of great importance and that, particularly as it affects cancer research, it is under active consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Our worthy deputy chairman has been closely associated with a hospital in his own constituency, and I understand he has a daughter who is a nurse and a son-in-law who practices as a surgeon at Kamloops-Doctor Verrett, a returned soldier and former student of Doctor Gallie's. I have not had his consent to mention this fact, but I take the liberty of doing so.
Under a zoning system a young doctor who knows something about surgery would be most useful, and the poor people throughout the country would get some relief. Consider the Indians for a moment; they were here two hundred years before the English or the French, but they have not even yet any doctors or nurses to attend to their needs. In fact we have been trying for two years-to find out if they are citizens. The fact is that they were citizens long ago, and if that is so they ought to be given this service automatically.
I do hope the minister will consider this matter seriously during the recess. I am hopeful that in the supplementary estimates, before the close of the session, he will announce some kind of grant to men of science like Doctor Best, and many others. There are two or three such men at McGill and at Toronto and other universities, and there are men right across Canada engaged in medical science who could do this work.
In recent years, medical science, the brightest child of all the sciences, has made remarkable strides, with the result that today the life expectancy has been increased to the extent of ten or fifteen years. This has been brought about mainly through the development of preventive medicine, new scientific methods and new methods of surgery. I hope that instead of operating only a skeleton department which used to spend about a half a million dollars before the war,. the department will take a more active interest and expand accordingly. Before the war France and Germany operated under a plan whereby, instead of permitting their medical students to work on boats, or as cooks or in other occupations, during the summer months, they were conscripted by the state to help in scientific work. We can take a leaf out of their book in that regard and, instead of permitting these young students to do outside
Supply-Health and Welfare

work during the summer and then go to the United States, have them do some work connected with medical science.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
216.	Distribution of drugs under regulations approved by the governor in council, $50,000.

Was the full amount
spent?

speakerposition: stagedirection

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
217.	Health insurance studies, $27,863.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement with respect to this item?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As a result of the action taken in 1941 this matter was given some measure of positive form in the proposals made by the government to the provinces in August 1945. Since that time we have had a director of health services who has just resigned from his post to take up another important task. At the present time the work is being carried on by a number of Individuals in our own department who I believe are specially qualified to deal with the matter. They have other functions as well. As a matter of fact only this morning I was hoping to be able to conclude certain arrangements with another department of government to enlist the services of a gentleman who I believe, because of his studies and his own experience, can be said to be exceptionally qualified in the field of health insurance. I am hoping he will be able to come to us to carry on and to supplement some of the work done by Doctor Little, by our own deputy minister and by several research assistants. I hope that within a week or so, in the person of Doctor H. M. Cassidy of the university of Toronto, we shall have the temporary services-I trust they will prove more than temporary-of one of the outstanding persons in this field in Canada. Arrangements have not yet been completed, but we are anxious to have his services to pass upon certain projects which I believe will prove important in the field of health insurance.
I assure the hon. member that this matter is being actively pursued. Apart from cancer and what we hope to do in respect of arthritis, this matter is receiving priority of interest so far as I am concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I consider that a most unsatisfactory statement from the minister. Last year there was an appropriation of 843,555, and this year in the estimates there is a
reduction of about *15,000. The sort of project the minister has outlined is not worth even the 827,863 mentioned in the item.
I hold in my hand the report of the advisory committee on health insurance appointed by order in council in 1942. I shall not take the time of the committee to read it, but it does provide some valuable material. The taxpayers of Canada have been at considerable expense in carrying out these surveys. The hopes of our people were raised when the representatives of so many different organizations were brought to Ottawa to give their opinions on the compilation of this information. Included in these were the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Nurses Association, the Canadian Hospital Council, the Canadian Dental Association, the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, and a whole list of other associations I shall not mention. They went to considerable expense to express their views, and I believe the taxpayers of Canada are entitled to know what happened to their ideas. What precisely has the department done this year? Who are devoting full time to this work? What has been done or what may we expect to be done with the $27,863 in the vote? What have we to show for what has been done? The minister should' give the committee more information than he has given thus far.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I regret that the hon. member thinks our active interest in pursuing these studies is not adequate. I do not know what more one can do than constantly engage one's attention on the problem. Instead of confining it as it originally was to one person, the work has been distributed to a number of people in the department who I believe are specially' competent. If the hon. gentleman wishes confirmation of that I would ask him to talk to Doctor Mott in Saskatchewan to ascertain if we in the department are not meeting this problem in a whole-hearted and embracing way. The decreases to which the hon. member has referred are in the educational and informational publicity item and1 other pay list items. That has nothing to do with the importance of the work. I venture to suggest that in the person of the present deputy of welfare we have a gentleman who has had tremendous experience with the only health insurance act ever passed by any government in this country. I have every reason to rely upon his judgment and skill in the matter. As I said a moment ago, I am hoping to have additional services on a temporary basis, because he is now permanently engaged, in the person of Doctor H. M. Cassidy. He was deputy' minister in the

Supply-Health and Welfare
appropriate department in British Columbia when the health insurance act was passed in that province some years ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am not criticizing any of the personnel. I am simply saying that this sort of report is not good enough. I have the greatest confidence in the deputy minister of the welfare branch, as well as of the health branch and other personnel. However, I submit that if we are spending $27,000 there should be some persons devoting their full time to the work. If the expenditures are being reduced at the rate of $15,000 a year it would indicate that the federal government is going out of the field of health insurance studies. The minister should tell us how many in this department have been working on this, how much was spent last year, and who are the persons employed on a full time basis.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are ten in the department working on it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think we are entitled to a break-down. How much was spent of the $43,000 which was voted last year? Who were the persons who were engaged on this work, and what were their duties?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The hon. member wdll recall that the department had only recently come into being at the time the estimate was prepared, and for the available personnel outside the department it was an overestimate. I can only repeat that we are engaging the full time of at least six persons in the department, with four additional persons who have other duties to perform. When we have the type of conference with the provinces which we envisage'we shall be prepared at that conference to submit details in respect to the studies we have been making and are making and to bring about at the earliest possible moment the realization of a health insurance scheme.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Last year the minister's predecessor was open to a great deal of criticism for asking for votes which in the opinion of some hon. members had no relation to the amounts which were to be expended. I have asked the minister a fair question: How much of the $43,000 which was voted for this purpose last year was spent, and how was it spent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There was spent $4,763.44.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like the
minister to explain why, if they estimated they were going to need $43,000 and spent only S4,700, they are now coming to parliament and asking for $27,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The division was created in December 1945, and the estimate was made in November 1945.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If you estimated in November 1945 you were going to spend $43,000, why was only $4,700 spent? How many are on the staff now, and what are the prospects of expending the $27,000 the minister is asking for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I can only say that we have ten people now on the staff who are engaged in- this work. Some of those people are doing other work as well. To the extent of the available personnel covered by non-filled posts at the moment we will spend this money. My hon. friend, considering the province from which he comes, should be in a special position to know that personnel in this particular field is extremely difficult to obtain. That has been experienced 'by the government of Saskatchewan, and we have had the same difficulty. The director left for another post, and an acting director was appointed1 in January. That gentleman has taken on a post which he regards as more important at the moment, that of acting secretary of the National Cancer Institute. But that in no way represents a diminution of the work, because, as I have indicated, the officials in our department, in our research division, the deputy minister and another gentleman whom we hope to have from another department, along with the services of Doctor Cassidy, will all be available.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not think the minister is giving the committee the sort of information it should have. The fact that there have been directors who have left for more important work indicates that this branch is not doing anything. In view of the general interest across the country and the representations which were made to the social security committee, I think it can be taken that the taxpayers in Canada consider this department quite seriously. They felt that they are going to get some active leadership in working out plans. I know there is no sure way from where you are to where you want to go, but the federal government should be giving some dynamic leadership across the country and trying to work out ways and means. The minister should tell us who in the department are devoting full time to this work. What are the names and qualifications of those who are directing this important branch?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Before the minister

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This matter is one that
comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces. It is one which they jealously guard as being within their own field. We did, however, in 1945 set up this division for the first time, at their request, as a sort of pooling agency to keep the provinces informed of what each was doing and to carry on general inspection work. The mental health field includes preventive work as well as provision for treatment facilities. The matter, of course, is a function of the provinces. The federal division cooperates with them in their efforts to benefit the mental hospital patients by surveying hospitals and setting up standards. We have produced a number of films at the request of the provinces, the cost of which we have borne. For instance, one film deals with the treatment of persons who have been in such institutions, the suggestion being that we should not frown upon such individuals but should try to help them. One film aims at increasing appreciation on the part of the public of the need of early treatment of mental illnesses, while another has reference to mild nervous and mental illness and the instructions of personnel engaged in the treatment of the mentally ill. There is another which deals with the treatment of children. As my hon. friend knows, there are many children in this country, as there are elsewhere, who are incipient patients. We try by educational methods, through films, lectures and the like, at the request of the provinces, to bring home to the people throughout Canada the dangers and ways and means of perhaps avoiding serious mental illnesses. That is the kind of work we are carrying on, and while the division has been in existence only since 1945, a truly remarkable job has been done, to use the words of Doctor Phair, deputy minister of health for Ontario. I look forward, as I am sure the hon. gentleman does, to greatly increased activity in this field, without any interference with the field occupied by the provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
While I quite agree with the minister that provincial mental institutions have been and are now being operated by the provincial governments, he knows, and I think the whole house knows, that practically all provincial governments are having considerable difficulty in operating modern mental institutions with proper facilities with the funds which are available for that sort of service. It seems to me most appropriate at this time that we should bring to the attention of the minister and of the government the great need of a comprehensive preventive and treatment programme for mental disease. I for one do not pose as an expert or an authority on this subject. I wish the minister to know that before I start. Nevertheless I should like to say a few words with regard to the difficulties which the provinces are now having in conducting mental institutions in a satisfactory manner.
I think it is generally recognized that mental disorders, wherein personality and behaviour may be profoundly affected are responsible for more chronic invalidism than any other disability. I believe the public is becoming increasingly aware of this problem. It has been repeatedly stated by those who know the subject well that mental derangements are not diminishing but are on the increase. As an indication of the extent and trend of the mental hygiene problem, according to a report from the bureau of statistics, patients in Canadian mental institutions increased from
25,000	in 1931 to 50,000 in 1946. A good deal of this increase is undoubtedly due to mental illness which comes about by old age and which has shown a considerable increase in the past decade or so because our population is getting older. The capacity of our mental institutions is inadequate to meet the needs of this increasing trend. The normal bed capacity at December 31, 1944, was 42,500 in the Dominion of Canada, according to the "Canada Year Book." During that same year there were 51,776 patients in mental hospitals or out on parole. Many on parole, of course, were less serious cases; but they were only on parole, I am informed, because they could not be accommodated in the institutions which we have. This indicates a serious overcrowded condition. Our mental institutions are inadequate for our needs. Most of them are understaffed and all too few of them are modern in either their construction or the equipment 
they operate. Mr. D. M. LeBourdais, who was referred to in the house the other day- he is, I believe, a lecturer and author of some note; at any rate, he served for some six years on the national committee for mental hygiene-has stated in no uncertain terms that Canada is failing in its duty toward the folk who are unfortunate enough to be inmates of our mental institutions. I believe this man speaks with some authority, Mr. Chairman, because he has inspected every Canadian institution devoted to the treatment of mental disease or mental ailments, as well as many in the United States. He states that most of our provincial mental institutions are obsolete.

The minister suggested that under this item I might raise the question of the facilities that exist for examination into possible remedies for cancer. If I might broaden the matter slightly I would mention what is also in the minds of a great many hon. members of the house, the fact that certain remedies have been suggested by men who believe they are of real value, who are having considerable difficulty getting them before the public. One case in point, which I think already has been brought to the attention of the minister, is that of Doctor Holder of Windsor, who fervently and ardently believes he has discovered the cause of cancer and various other serious ills and a method of treatment for those maladies which may mean the saving of thousands of lives in this country.
We have another case in point, which I think probably all hon. members have had brought to their attention; that is Doctor Koch's remedy for various ills. In my constituency there are people who believe they have been cured by Doctor Koch's treatment of ills that have successfully resisted every other kind of treatment. I should like to ask the minister whether he has a committee or some other facility whereby ideas which are new can be examined objectively and thoroughly so those who believe in the ideas will have every opportunity to demonstrate, to their own satisfaction, everything in favour of their cause. Has he any facility whereby all the evidence may be recorded and reports submitted which would be entirely objective and unbiased, reports which could come before the public of Canada and the members of this house so we might have a chance of studying these suggestions with some hope of arriving at a sound conclusion? Would the minister tell us something about such facilities, if we have them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
brought this up the other evening, and I asked him to wait for this item. I thank him for

Supply-Health and Welfare

having done so. Mr. Holder of the city of Windsor is well known to me. He is a very estimable gentleman, who has written a textbook as well as several articles on this subject. When I saw him last, which was three or four weeks ago, following certain correspondence, I referred him to the proper agency in Ontario, the commission for investigation of cancer remedies. That commission has investigated a number of proposed treatments for cancer. Since I have been minister two others have come to my attention, and I want to say to the hon. gentleman that I think the proper attitude to take, and this is the attitude I am taking, is that if anyone thinks he has a solution, regardless of what others may think about it is in the absence of an investigation, certainly I should not let any stone remain unturned to give that person an opportunity to have his suggestion investigated. Just to give an example, last week a doctor from a certain town in this province came to see me. I had representations by certain other practitioners in reference to this particular gentleman, representations that could hardly be said to be complimentary to the individual concerned. I was not in a position to pass on the merits of the case, but I did take steps at once to make sure that the commission to investigate cancer remedies was given a chance to do so, and that body is also going to investigate this matter. In other words if a suggestion comes to us we point out that the matter comes under provincial jurisdiction and that the province should have an opportunity first to go into the matter. I assure my hon. friend that no one in this country who has a suggestion to, offer will be turned away from my door. I could mention another case. I do not think I had better mention the name of the person, but he is well known in Ontario, and claims to have cured people. I had better not identify him beyond that, because it would not be fair to him. I can say however that he is a gentleman who has been considerably in the public eye. He proposes setting up an institution in this province at his own expense for clinical treatment. I do not know whether he has a cure. I have also seen to it that that gentleman is not being denied the opportunity of a full investigation of his claims. That will be my attitude.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I congratulate the
minister upon what he has said. I am positive that many good ideas have been neglected because people in high places have not taken the unbiased view the minister has just expressed. Has the minister taken the precaution to see that reports of investigations are accurately made? I have known cases in which

reports have been so garbled as to give an altogether erroneous impression as to what actually took place upon investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have designated one
official in my department, who after such requests have come in and we have asked the proper agency to look into it, will follow up so as to make sure he is satisfied this has been done. I am satisfied that is being done not only with regard to cancer but in other matters.
May I add that only a short time ago I read in the press that an old classmate of mine, whom I had not seen for a number of years, in collaboration with some other physicians, had developed a pill which he said was a cure for certain types of heart disease. I do not know whether it is or not. However I did know this man. At university I found him sincere and hard working; and if what he had perfected could be the means of giving relief to someone I thought he should be given the opportunity to show its worth. He was complaining that he was not being given a chance to put forward his formula. I wrote to him and went myself to see him in London, just to ascertain whether he had any particular grievance. He told me what the situation was. I got in touch with the minister of health for Ontario and I found he had anticipated anything I was doing in the matter and was giving it his full attention. As it was one which came properly within the provincial field, there was nothing further for me to do except to be satisfied that it was being looked into.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I cannot resist the invitation given by the minister to offer a suggestion with respect to a matter which would come within his jurisdiction. I am not quite sure whether what I have in mind should come under this item, or might more properly be discussed under the item for grants. It has to do with the control of tuberculosis.
Each year around Christmas time the various tuberculosis associations in Canada issue Christmas seals from the sale of which they are interested in obtaining as much money as possible. I am told the government is interested in having Christmas correspondence, including greeting cards, placed in the mails as early as possible, and that the earlier this is done the greater is the economy effected. I suggest that the minister have a conference with the Postmaster General with a view to setting aside one or two days early in, December in which all letters and parcels with Christmas seals as stamps could be passed through the post office. I believe these Christ-

Supply-Health and Welfare
mas seals are the only ones of their kind now distributed or made available to the public. The various tuberculosis societies would immensely increase their stamp sales, and the public in general, by buying these seals at one cent each, would economize by placing them on their Christmas cards and parcels. Then the government would have an interest in getting the mail in as early as possible and an economy would be effected.
In various other countries other means have been found of doing the same thing. For instance, in Cuba everyone is obliged during November and December to place an additional stamp on each letter. I understand) that in Switzerland during the Christmas season they sell a stamp for, I believe, one half more than the current stamps. The people may take either the special tuberculosis stamps, or the others which are sold at a lower price, and the amount collected by the government on those stamps is given to the tuberculosis societies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for what I believe is a constructive suggestion. I shall see to it at once that at the earliest opportunity the hon. member, the Postmaster General and myself have an opportunity to discuss the matter with a view to seeing, if the suggestion could be carried out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was particularly pleased to hear what the minister said in reply to the hon. member for Lethbridge. While his remarks were directed more particularly to tuberculosis, the minister did say that not only in respect of cancer, but also in other respects, he was giving, attention to any possible, cure which might be advanced for other diseases. That was much more encouraging than the reply I received from his predecessor last year, when I referred to a doctor in Chicago who claimed he had some special knowledge about arthritis. The minister will understand I am not attempting to speak as an expert, but I am simply offering him some of the information I have gained from correspondence. I have learned that there is a Doctor Golden in Chicago who has made a study of arthritis- and perhaps the minister has checked on this. I should like to hope that he has, or that he will do so.
I would bring to the minister's attention another matter which in medical and other circles is highly controversial. I refer to practice by chiropractors. I know that any mention of a chiropractor to a qualified medical practitioner will make him laugh. I am not an expert in these matters; I go to either of them as infrequently as possible, and hope I shall not have to go any more frequently in 83166-283i
the future than I have in the past. I do know however that many people believe they get relief and even cures from the operations of chiropractors. This belief is too widespread among lay citizens for me to brush it aside, and to say that because the medical doctors say the chiropractors are no good, therefore they must be no good. Has the minister's department given attention to this matter, and has the minister any information which he could give the committee? Does the department purpose carrying out any investigation with a view to letting the public know what its opinion is about this type of practitioner?-.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member will know, of course, that the matter of chiropractors comes within the control of the provinces. I would not want to interfere in that field.
As the hon. member may recall, I said the other evening when the name of Doctor Golden was mentioned that after the consultations Dr. Moore of this department has had with Lord Horder, the great rheumatics expert of Great Britain, in collaboration with Doctor Wallace Graham of Toronto we have decided to call a conference within a short time of the arthritic and rheumatic experts in the country to see if we cannot go into this whole problem. The proposal of Doctor Golden in regard to arthritis treatment is a matter which will not be overlooked at that time. When the hon. member drew a comparison between myself and my predecessor I am sure he did not mean what he said, because every day I am finding proof in the department of the devoted service in the field of health and welfare rendered by my predecessor, the Minister of National Defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I meant no reflection upon the minister. I simply wanted to point out that when I asked if any consideration was being given to Doctor Golden's suggestion the answer was an abrupt "no" which was extremely unsatisfactory. With regard to chiropractors, I appreciate the minister's statement that the issuing of licences granting the right to practise is entirely in the hands of the provincial governments, but I was wondering if the department was considering issuing advisory statements-not that they should or should not be but simply to give some idea of whether their work is really worth while. You would not be imposing a federal order upon the provincial governments; it would simply be a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What medical services are provided for the Indians and Eskimos, and do they include dental services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What other services are
provided?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member has been a distinguished member of the Indian affairs committee under the chairmanship of my colleague, the hon. member for Essex West. I have been following the work of that committee, and I think the committee will understand me when I say that I am proud of my colleague, the hon. member for Essex West, for the work he has done as chairman of that committee. The Indian health services became a division of the Department of National Health and Welfare in November, 1945. Prior to that the services were under the Department of Mines and Resources. The aim of the Indian health services division is to provide and complete a health service to all Indians and Eskimos who are wards of the dominion government. For this purpose hospital, nursing and ancillary services have been organized. The division's facilities are not only devoted to providing general medical and surgical services, but special attention is being directed to the treatment of tuberculosis and venereal diseases. I need not tell the committee that the tubercular mortality rate among Indians is higher than one would like to see it. When one considers the projects that have been under way since 1938 one realizes that the great improvement in attacking this problem has by no means been a complete improvement. I myself plan this summer to visit as many of the stations as I possibly can-not that my presence will do much, but I wish to form an impression in relation to some important decisions which are suggested by the officers of my department. We have under way several projects for hospitals a swell as other projects actually in progress looking to improvement of methods by which we can deal with the health of the Indians. The hon. gentleman from his experience on the Indian affairs committee will undoubtedly be able to confirm my view that because of the dispersal of the Indians and Eskimos often in inaccessible areas the service in some regions is far from perfect. I am not saying that in criticism of my officers, because I do not think I could have under me any more devoted officers, and certainly no more devoted director than the present incumbent. But the Indian is nomadic. He does not always live in well settled areas. The situation cannot be materially improved until modern transportation facilities are integrated into the health service, and we are giving consideration to means of providing under our own control a better air transport service to deal with the transfer of Indian patients to centres where they can get medical attention, and also for the purpose of moving our own men.
In addition to the construction of hospital units and the conversion of hospitals such as the one at Qu'Appelle, we have in some instances given a grant for example, to the sanatorium at Fort William, to undertake the special treatment of Indians. We have no constitutional way of giving such assistance to hospitals in various municipalities and provinces, but as the Indian is our ward, sometimes rather than build a hospital we do give financial assistance to institutions such as I have mentioned where the Indians are treated. Likewise we have arrangements with smaller institutions throughout all parts of Canada to render medical assistance. I assure the committee that we are accelerating our effort in a field in which we have full jurisdiction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the board of our sanatorium in Fort William, where we have a hospital that deals not only with Fort William but with all western Ontario, I want to say that when two members of the board came down here they were treated not only courteously but generously, and they went back encouraged in the belief that the department of health of the dominion government was behind them in their work. They 'had to build a large addition to the hospital, with the assistance of the provincial and federal governments, to provide facilities for the Indians to be treated in the most modern way. On behalf of the board I wish to express my appreciation of the minister's efforts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Along with other members of the house I welcome the increased expenditures which the minister is going to make on the Indians. Hon. members who are on the Indian affairs committee have an advantage over other hon. members in that they have been able to get to the bottom of the grievances respecting medical services to the Indians. We had Doctor Moore and other members of the department under cross-examination by the committee for a few days.
The addition of the Indian health services to the Department of National Health and Welfare is something new which is going to be watched very carefully. The Indians in Canada for the last forty or fifty years have been a neglected people, and anybody who has the welfare of the Indian at heart wel-
Supply-Health and Welfare

comes this new approach. But care must be taken that the Indian health services do not become a mere sideline of the new department. I hope that the minister will promise us that this will not happen so long as he is in charge of this department, but that the Indian will get equal treatment with the white man so far as medical services are concerned.
This vote of $4,000,000 looks a large amount; but remember that the Indians have been neglected for forty years, and this is only what is coming to them, to do for them what you would expect Canada to do for the Indians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What progress has been made in establishing the Indian hospital at North Battleford, and what is the staff there, if it is now operating?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The Battleford hospital is suitable for about fifty beds. This can be provided in the buildings erected in conjunction with the former R.C.A.F. field at North Battleford. Alterations are required to provide for the isolation of tuberculosis patients and proper accommodation for the staff. There are no suitable quarters for the staff at the hospital, but we have engineers up there who are expeditiously, in the light of material shortages, trying to complete the work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will it be ready for winter occupation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: By September 1, I hope.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was delighted to hear the minister say that he was going to visit as many reserves as possible this year. I want to take this opportunity to invite him to Qu'Appelle valley, and will be very happy to act as guide for him. I think it is a reflection on our treatment of the Indians that the death rate from tuberculosis among the Indians is twenty times as high as it is among the white people in our province, which has established a world record in reducing the mortality rate. I think the minister will soon realize that the health of the Indians is bound up with nutrition, housing and employment. Their health is a reflection of the economic position of the family. I can take the minister to one family after another who are sheltering the grandparents, and where members of two and three generations are housed in one room under one roof. I can take him to old people who cannot afford coal oil and who are gnawing crusts because there is no old age pension for the Indians. We must not only talk about the health of the Indians; we must consider how we can help them establish a higher income, how we can help the Indian to rehabilitate himself and his family so that

he can have better housing and better nutrition, which will be reflected in the health records of the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I agree with what the hon. member has said. I could not ignore her very kind offer of guidance. I may tell her that except in the matter of political guidance I shall be glad to accept her kind offer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall be glad to help the minister there too.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. lady's observations will be noted by many of us, but I can assure her also that the problem is a difficult one, to help those who apparently cannot help themselves. why it is under a separate heading of cash allowances instead of being included under the heading of salaries and wages.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The biggest item of
all is $2 million in connection with professional and special services. Can the minister give a breakdown or explanation of that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The amount of $2 million is required to cover cost of services of doctors, dentists, nurses not on salary, hospitalization and special charges for all treatment carried out by other than departmental institutions. The increase is due to the enhanced health consciousness of the population and the advent of new and expensive drugs such as penicillin, as well as the persistent rise in hospital rates all across the dominion. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I suggest that in

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I would bring to your attention, as well as the attention of the Minister of Public Works, the fact that on this side we are annoyed by a terrible draught. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I agree that there is something in what the hon. gentleman has said, but he should take it up with the Minister of Public Works, who, I have no doubt, will give the matter consideration. I would, however, remind the hon. and kindly gentleman that we are discussing the item on Indians.

speechtext: What the hon. gentleman said comes aptly under health and welfare.

Dear Sir:

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The rates asked by the institutions vary from as low as $2.50 a day to as high as $8. Many institutions accept an inclusive rate for all ordinary hospital services. Others claim extra payment over and above the per diem rate. In all cases the department is endeavouring to establish an all inclusive per diem rate. As the hon. gentleman knows, hospitalization costs have risen rapidly in the last year or so. As I have said, the costs have varied. There are some districts where the cost is terrifically high, because of long hauls to get supplies in, and so on. Factors affecting this rise are the increasing cost of commodities, the adoption of the eight-hour day for nurses, the organization of hospital employees into organizations of their own, resulting in marked salary increases. I have been discussing the matter with a number of officials. Only the other day I had a long talk with Bishop Renison of the James Bay district, who has had tremendous experience there. I have discussed it with others as well, and I can say the whole problem now is under study and adjustment. Any institution asking for an increase in rates is asked to submit a statement of per diem costs for public ward patients, and some explanation as to how these are computed. The regional superintendents are instructed to visit any hospitals asking for increases, to meet the hospital authorities and discuss rates with them, and to report back on the facilities provided for the treatment of Indians. We then attempt to strike what we think is a just and equitable rate. I recall the matter my hon. friend has brought to my attention, and I may assure him it is receiving my very active attention.

This is a new item and I suppose the minister will have an explanation to give to the committee. Apparently this arises out of the research that was done during the war. There does not seem to be a head for this department and all the assistance seems to be of a temporary nature.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend will understand that under the rules of the civil service a man is appointed temporarily for a probationary period. This is a new division and obviously you could not hajve anything but temporaries. For example, the new director, Doctor Emard of Cornwall, has just received his appointment from the civil service commission, and he will continue as temporary chief until he is confirmed in the position.
This is a new division created at the instance of the Department of Transport, which felt that they were in urgent need of medical advice for setting physical standards for civil flying personnel and for organizing and training medical service personnel to examine all prospective employees in civil aviation. It would assist in all medical examinations and advise on the suitability of applicants for employment from both mental and physical points of view. It would advise on all health problems connected with travel by air and would supervise industrial medical services at airports.
It was felt by both this department and by the Department of Transport that this division should be set up within the Department of National Health and Welfare. The purpose in this arrangement is to enable the medical officers to be closely associated with other medical officers in the public health service of the dominion government. They will attend staff meetings and take part in professional discussions; they will use the medical library and attend conferences of representatives of the various departments concerned with this endeavour.
Supply-Health and Welfare

It was thought that by this arrangement we can facilitate the close association which should be maintained between the new division, existing divisions, especially immigration medical services. I am sure the committee will appreciate that, with the advent of air travel by people from all parts of the world, there is a danger that these people will be potential vehicles for the communication of diseases of one kind and another. The closest attention and scrutiny must be given to those travelling by air, as is given to travellers on incoming vessels.

It would be interesting
to know the extent to which there will be cooperation between this new branch and the work in connection with civil aviation which was carried on by the R.C.A.F. medical branch during the war. This country has every reason to be proud of the work of that branch. We would want to be assured that there will be the closest cooperation between this new branch and the R.C.A.F. institute of aviation medicine in my riding and that, as far as possible, personnel for this department will be recruited from those who served with the medical branch of the R.C.A.F. during the war. The minister has referred to the qualifications of Doctor Emard, and I am sure the committee would be interested in knowing something of his relationship.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
During the war Doctor
Emard was a R.C.A.F. doctor with distinguished service. After the war he had experience as head of one of the important hospitals in Quebec operated by D.V.A. As I say, he served in the R.C.A.F. and has a distinguished record. The liaison between the research division of the R.C.A.F. and this branch is not only one of intention; it is one that is actually in being. We shall work closely together for the reasons so well stated by the hon. gentleman.

What salary will he
receive?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
There is an item for
travelling expenses, and in going through all the items for the department I find that travelling expenses total about half a million dollars. That seems a rather large item for one department of government in peace time and I wonder if we could have an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is a large item, but
that is necessarily so, and I think the hon. gentleman will appreciate that when he realizes the type of services rendered by all branches of the department. For instance, there are expenses in connection with servicing

the Department of Mines and Resources immigration branch, both abroad and at home ports. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Will the minister give
us some information with respect to the details given on page 175 of the estimates? There is an item, temporary assistance, $10,992. This is the last item on the medical side of this department. Can the minister now give us the total expenditure for the year from the total 1946-47 estimate of $7,651,252? Second, he was going to give the actual expenditure under item 200, departmental administration. Third, what was the total amount spent by the department last year on educational and informational publicity?

What are the outstanding commitments?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have not got them but I will get them.

There was one other matter on which the minister was going to give some

detail, and that was with regard to arthritis. He said on June 19, at page 4007 of Hansard:
The hon. member referred to arthritis, and perhaps later in the estimates I shall have more to say about this specific item.
The minister has already announced that there is to be a conference, but apparently one of the grave problems is hospital accommodation. I understand that only one hospital in Canada specializes in treating rheumatic diseases. Are any plans made for improving the hospitalization situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That whole matter will be discussed at the conference which is to take place very shortly, following our consultations with Lord Horder and Doctor Wallace Graham in Toronto.
Has nothing been done to increase the hospital facilities for this disease since last year?

When will the conference be held?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am hoping that it will be in September. I should like to have it before that, but certain arrangements have to be made with certain people whom we want to attend.
What class of hospitals are exempt from sales tax on their supplies?

Why are not the supplies of private hospitals where the same treatment is given exempt?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The item we are considering is civil aviation medicine.
