On a former occasion we had a lengthy discussion regarding postwar plans, but the minister at that time was
not prepared to indicate what plans his department had for the next two years or so. Can he make a general statement now with regard to major projects which he plans undertaking over a period of years?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
During the year we tried to add to the staff of architects and engineers, but we are finding it difficult to keep even the staff we have now. Young engineers and architects seem to prefer private enterprise. The staff we have at the present time is working on plans for buildings throughout the country to meet the needs of different departments. The engineers are also working on plans for works on both coasts and along the great lakes and the St. Lawrence. Last fall I travelled from Ottawa to the western coast to see the conditions for myself.
There is no doubt that we lack office space for nearly every department in nearly every province. We also lack facilities on the coasts, but we have found that lack of material and of staff in the preparation of plans and specifications has hindered the progress which we should like to make. Furthermore, lack of materials and of man-power has also in many instances prevented us from proceeding with the works we had contemplated even in the main estimates. If hon. gentlemen will look over my estimates they will see that in connection with certain specified projects the word "revote" appears. The amount of money was granted by parliament last year, but we could not complete the plans and specifications in time, and often, when we did complete them, after asking for tenders we found that we could not get any bids. That condition existed in many parts of the country. This year we are asking parliament for the same votes, perhaps with some increase, but the increases in the main estimates of public works-
They are less than $5 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Yes, $3 million odd. The reason for the increase in the vote is, first, maintenance of public buildings in Ottawa, which is due mainly to reconversion from war to peace-time status. Many of these buildings, before the present year, were maintained out of appropriations under demobilization or war appropriations. They have been transferred to the main estimates. The second reason would be maintenance of public buildings outside Ottawa, owing to increase in salaries caused by absorption of cost of living bonus, as well as provision for 207 new positions and an increase in the salary range of various classes of employees. The third reason for the increase would be in the general pro-
Supply-Public Works

vincial repair appropriations for buildings and harbours necessitated by lack of repairs during the six years of war. We have increased that amount so that we can try this year at least to maintain our works in satisfactory repair condition. The fourth reason is that we have new items, totalling less than half a million dollars.
This year we expect that the situation as regards materials will ease up, and with a few additions to our staff we may be able to complete certain plans and specifications and proceed with certain works. I do not like to come before parliament with estimates of large amounts and next year come back and ask for a revote, but everyone will agree that my department is working under extraordinary conditions. If we were to proceed with a large programme of buildings-and I heard this all over the country-the first thing that would be said would be that this is no time to start large projects in view of the fact that materials are needed for housing, especially for veterans.
We have found that the increase in prices today is such that we might make an estimate in November or December, and later on, when we ask for bids, the tender would be far above the estimate we had made four or five months ahead of time. The department is not definite as to how much progress can be made even with the plans we have prepared right now. The department has to rely on the reports given by other departments, such as reconstruction, with respect to availability of materials, labour and man-power to carry out the works.
Mr. MaoNICOL: Will the minister tell the committee exactly what part his department plays in the general construction of works for all departments? During the last few hours we have heard a good deal about hospitalization, and I gathered from what was said that an architectural department will be set up in the branch which we were discussing. I was under the impression all the time that when hospitals or any other buildings under the federal government were needed-I do not mean large construction works-the departments concerned made a requisition to the architectural branch of the Public Works Department to draw up the necessary plans. Will the minister tell us what relation the Department of Public Works has to all the other departments as far as constructing public buildings is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
We do undertake and execute works for every department. I may make an exception of the armed forces. The national defence department have a
(Mr. Fournier.]
branch dealing with their own buildings apart from buildings for office space. Another exception is reconstruction. They do works themselves through their own crown-owned companies. The ordinary departments of government, however, come to the Department of Public Works. Take, for instance, health and welfare. If they need hospitals for Indians they get a vote for the purpose and make a transfer to public works. In cooperation with the architect they have at the head of the hospital designs branch of that department, we prepare plans or have an outside architect, under our supervision, prepare them. Outside public works, you will find, in external affairs, for instance, an architect who travels around and looks after our buildings outside this country. There are a few architects in the veterans affairs department who are also interested in hospital designing and the supervision of the different buildings they need for the care of veterans. I cannot recall whether there are other departments which have architects. Those are the three main departments. In health and welfare, notably, they have one architect who has specialized in hospital designing. I do not know whether he makes designs himself, but he is the kind of expert adviser we would have to prepare plans for hospitals. That is, as I see it, the justification for this special branch in health and welfare, especially since they have taken over Indian affairs hospitalization.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, because I for one was alarmed, in view of what we heard this afternoon, that other departments would set up their own architectural staffs. In the old days and all down through the years, to my knowledge-and I used to have a good deal to do with the public works department, particularly the architectural branch-the Department of Public Works made all the plans for the public buildings of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
We do all this work of making the plans and specifications through our architect's branch in the Department of Public Works. I believe it was only during the war that this situation has come to the fore and that certain men having these special qualifications have been taken on. But still, when these departments do propose any works, this architect in the Department of National Health and Welfare would be the man who would be the liaison officer with our own department to explain the things they need and the way they would like to have the plans prepared. I do not believe it would be a good policy to extend appointments of architects to every department.

Supply-Public Works
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am glad to have my hon. friend's advice on that. I am convinced that in our department we have experienced men.
The very best.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: They are men who have been in construction work for years and years. They are trained. Some of them have spent their lives in the department and have an experience which no ordinary architect in private practice would have. I do not consider that these departments should try to take over and divide up the architect's branch of the Department of Public Works; but in certain instances, for special work such as hospitals, I think there is no harm in having a man to advise the minister concerned as to modern developments in the construction of hospitals. I believe he would be a help to our own architects in that special line. Once again, let me say that I do not believe it should become the practice of dividing up the architects branch among the departments.

From years of experience, I can say that the Department of Public Works has excellent engineers in all the various branches, such as heating, ventilating, air conditioning, and everything pertaining to buildings. To me it would be too bad if other departments were setting up architects to carry on what the Department of Public Works is so well qualified to do, having such well qualified men in its architectural branch. I am glad to hear what the minister says.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I should not like to allow that remark to pass without joining in the sentiments and kind words of praise for our officials which the hon. member has expressed. He is someone who knows these officials. For five years I personally have had contact with them, and I tell not only my colleagues but many other people that I think we have the best civil servants in those two branches-engineers and architects-that can be found in the country.
There are none better.

I have a great number of immediate demands for public buildings. I have discussed the matter with the minister on several occasions, and he has been most kind and considerate in going over the possibilities with me. I appreciate the difficulties which he has in the matter of public buildings, particularly those which are caused by shortages in building material. Will he be good enough to make a statement as to the position of his department with respect to public
buildings? Is there any sign that in the near future he may be able to proceed with a greater programme of construction? I do not intend to give a list of the number of public buildings which are immediately necessary in the riding of Cariboo, but I would call to the minister's attention the requirements of the town of Clinton for a post office, of Williams Lake for a public building, and particularly of Quesnel for a public building. Since I have been on his doorstep for some years with regard to these public buildings, I should like the minister to make a statement so that the people of these towns and villages may have some understanding of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Actually the
government occupies 762 public buildings all through the country. They are government-owned buildings. We have leases of premises for ordinary departments in 597 buildings and leases for war purposes-that is, for offices occupied by departments which, we believe, will disappear as time goes by-in 147, making a total of 1,506 buildings all over the country. In my main estimates I have down, for every province, a large number of items for repairs or additions to our actual buildings all through the country. We tried to use that vote last year but have made very little progress because no one seems to want to bid on a firm basis. As you know, during the war many of the works were constructed on a cost-plus percentage or fee basis. Today contractors hesitate to tender firm bids because of the material situation, prices and even the labour situation. I am told that the contractors all over the country are so busy with work for private enterprise, which they prefer, and which they can generally have on a cost-plus basis, that they decline to tender on a firm basis. I wish to say here that even during the war the Department of Public Works -and I agree with my officials-would not change the procedure which has been established in that department for many decades, whereby they ask for tenders and give out the contracts to the lowest bidder. Contractors are beginning to come back-and I hope they will do so-to the idea that for government purposes that is still the best policy which can be followed. I say that without criticism of what was done by the government during the war. In normal times the only way to satisfy the public, when spending their money, is to give an equal chance to everybody to tender for the works which are to be undertaken. All through the country I have requests, not only from members, but from the various departments of
Supply-Public Works

government, and especially from my colleague the Postmaster General.
Is he worse than the rest?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I would not say worse, but I have a lengthy list from his department, endorsing requests made by members of parliament, not only on this side of the house, but on all sides. We cannot see our way clear during this fiscal year, however, to put up those buildings. We are trying to make a start. I have some estimates providing for the purchase of sites, in preparation for putting up these buildings, but as to the actual construction I am afraid I cannot assure the hon. gentleman that during this fiscal year we can expend even the sums contained in the estimates. I am told, however, that next year probably the material situation will have eased, and I am sure I shall have the support of all hon. members especially those who come to see me and ask me to put up buildings in their ridings, in putting through my estimates to give different communities the buildings they need for the public service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the questions the hon. member for Cariboo is asking, but perhaps he will follow on after I have asked one. The matter I am going to raise will not take very long. The question of new buildings across Canada, as the hon. member for Cariboo has pointed out, is important, but this afternoon I want to raise the question of caring for some of the buildings we already have. I refer particularly to the building in which we now sit. I want to protest against the condition of this chamber at this moment. It is not fair to ask hon. members to sit here with the draught we feel today. This matter was raised a short time ago by the hon. member for Queens. I wish some hon. gentlemen opposite could sit here and feel the draught on the back of our necks. I want to ask the minister who is responsible for the ventilation of this chamber; and, if it is his department, what steps have been taken to correct it. This is not the first time we have had this condition. It is a frequent occurrence, but today it is just a little worse than I have ever known it. I do not blame hon. members for leaving the chamber and refusing to sit here under these conditions. Would the minister explain why this cannot be corrected; or, if it can be corrected, why he does not take steps to have this done?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
After the complaint was made in the committee about an

hour ago, I made inquiries, but I received different reports. While sitting here, I received one report that an hon. member, coming into the building from the heat outside, just walked into the lobby and opened the windows. Is that correct? I do not know, but I have that information.
They are now closed.
Just sit here and feel the draught on your neck.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If you will give me time I will give the picture as it has been given to me. If it is true that the windows were opened I am afraid I cannot be on the job every moment telling the officials to close them. There is a ventilating system here; and I am told that today the officials put on the fans, in view of the heat outside. The moment the complaint was made, someone went down and turned off those fans.
But it is still blasting.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: But the effect does not disappear the moment you turn off the fans. Another person came in and told me that the moment you open the doors in the ladies' gallery, the wind blows from one end of the chamber to the other. There may be ten reasons why we are not comfortable, but we are constantly endeavouring to find ways and means of seeing to it that every member of parliament will feel comfortable at all times, on both sides of the chamber.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is this condition peculiar to this side of the house, or it is general? There is a strong draught on my back, and I assure the minister it is most objectionable. There should be some way to correct it. With a proper system of ventilation, we should not have to put up with such a condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am told that the exhaust fans are on that side of the house, I have just asked my deputy if he can correct that condition and he says probably they will have to be put on both sides.

Could the minister not
remove the vacuums which are on that side of the house, which would cause the draughts?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There is a draught on this side of the house as well. I know last evening the hon. member for Algoma East was sitting here and had to leave the chamber because of the draught. So it is not only on that side.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is an added reason, though not quite so important as the one I raised.

Supply-Public Works

This is not something that has happened recently. This draught has been very bad for the last month or more.
I have gone down and spoken to the engineer to see if the situation could be remedied, but apparently very little has been done. I just cannot stay in the chamber part of the time because of the tremendous draught over here. Anyone with asthma will feel it very badly.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: For many years I have not received so much support from an hon. member as I have within the past few moments from the hon. member for Carleton. I hope, when I bring in estimates involving the expenditure of large sums of money for all the public works suggested to me, he will continue his support. I thank him, right now.
I would always support the improvement of a dirty building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I agree that our buildings are in a poor condition. But let me remind the hon. member that at one time
Supply-Public Works

during the war years my estimates were down as low as $12 million or $13 million. All agreed at that time that our policy was a good one, and that during the war we should direct all our effort to the winning of the war. I recall days when my estimates would be passed in fifteen or twenty minutes, and that fact did not surprise me greatly because the committee was not agreeing to very much.
Now that the war is over, we are adding every year to the estimates and increasing the staff. In the city of Ottawa we own fifty-two buildings. But does the committee know how many buildings we rent in this city? We rent ninety-six buildings right in this city of Ottawa. That goes to show that the government does lack government-owned space. The right policy would be to have our own buildings in a good state of repair, and we are working toward that end.
My good friend chose about the oldest buildings when he was describing their poor condition. Some of them were built as far back as confederation.
Is it that long ago since the walls were cleaned?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Every government must take its share of responsibility for not having kept them in good condition. I have noticed this state of affairs; but, as the years go on, one of the buildings to which the hon. member referred will probably change some of its uses. At the present time it houses the Department of Finance, which has become most important. The time may come when it may require more space and will want to move somewhere else. We also have there the Department of External Affairs, which twenty years ago did not exist, but has now become most important. The privy council is lodged in the same building.
Our intention is to try to keep that building for the privy council, the Prime Minister's office and the Department of External Affairs. But we cannot so easily get rid of a department as important as the Department of Finance. We have not yet found a location which would suit the needs of that department.
However, I would not be discouraged. Anyone who will look into the work of this department will see that it is a most interesting one. It is not intellectual or spiritual; one gets right down to-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Dirt.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
earth. Every time a lavatory is not in working condition,

someone will be kind enough to tell the minister there is something wrong in his department. If a charwoman is sick, or there is some difficulty in connection with the payment of her wages, the minister will receive a letter; he will hear about it. And during all this time the thousands of employees in the department are doing their best, with the moneys available, to do their jobs.

I am not asking the minister to make any grandiose expenditures in Ottawa, nor am I asking him to erect new buildings. But if at the present time we cannot have new buildings, and cannot make large expenditures, at least we should keep the buildings we have in better condition than they are now being kept. Surely it would not take much money from the dominion treasury to clean or to redecorate the walls, and to improve the lighting facilities so as to make those buildings already constructed sanitary and healthful. That would not be difficult. I believe the minister agrees with me, but I do not like to have him suggest that I am asking for heavy expenditures when, in fact, I am asking only that the government maintain its present buildings in decent condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I go to the east block every day, and I know it well. I do not know if it would be worth while to clean the walls, because most of those walls should be torn down. It should be repartitioned or divided for the needs of the departments we shall have there. We could spend $20,000 or $25,000 on the building, but in a year or so we would have to tear some of those walls down. They are old buildings. That building would require complete reconstruction; we could keep the shell; probably, and build something new inside. That would not be a grandiose project; it would be useful, but it would cost a lot of money and require a lot of material.

Complaints have been made practically every session since I came here, and are still being made, about accommodation in this building. While those of us in the house are privileged to bring our complaints to the minister-even though he does not act upon them in all cases-there are others who cannot voice their complaints. I refer to the stenographic staff in this building, who are perhaps the right arms of the members. They, too, have complaints which reach the members from day to day, but wrhich have not yet been attended to. I understand that at the present time (heir working condi-

Supply-Public Works
tions are considerably worse than they have been for a number of years past. I do not know if anything is being done by the minister, but if nothing has been done I suggest that it should be. These people are expected to do their work efficiently, and they should have much better working conditions than they have at the present time.

I wish to compliment the engineers and fieldmen of the department who are operating in British Columbia. I believe they are closely connected with their problems, and are giving very satisfactory service. However I would make a criticism of the department's architectural branch in British Columbia. I am sure they are not fully aware of modern working conditions and the circumstances under which people in this day and age should be asked to work.
For a number of years I have followed closely the recommendations in British Columbia in connection with certain buildings and projects, and in my opinion the architectural staff of the department, as it operates in British Columbia, is old fashioned in methods, old fashioned in ideas, bureaucratic, and slower than molasses.
Let me give an illustration: For some years the accommodation in the public building at Trail has been most inadequate. A number of young girls employed in the post office found it necessary to eat their lunches in the building. The branch made a survey of the whole building, and it was then proposed by this branch that the girls should eat their lunches in the basement in which there is a continuous foul odour from the sewer. I should like the gentleman in question to eat his lunch there for a few months in succession.
Then I wish to complain about the lighting in these public buildings. I know two or three people whose eyesight has been badly effected by having to work under poor lights. I am referring particularly to the post offices at Trail and Nelson. At small expense the lighting in these buildings could be improved. People having to sort mail and work with figures are now forced to work under lights placed on high ceilings, and there is no necessity for that when a small expenditure would permit them to work under good lighting conditions.
I should also like to refer to the discrepancy in janitors' salaries. I have never been able to get the real basis upon which janitors are paid. In one place a man receives a higher salary for doing less than another man
receives for doing more. I urge an inquiry into these inequalities.
I urge the minister to check up on the architectural branch in British Columbia. I suggest that he visit, the province to see some of the things I have mentioned. I think my criticism is correct, that these officials are old fashioned in their ideas, bureaucratic in their methods and slower than molasses.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is the minister in a position to make a statement with regard to the negotiations in connection with the new post office in Winnipeg? I am not pressing that immediate action be taken, but there is keen interest in this matter and I hope the minister is ready to tell us whether a new site has been purchased and, if so, where it is. If a site has not been purchased, could he tell us whether the request of the greater Winnipeg town planning commission that they be consulted before the site is finally chosen has been acceded to?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I was in Winnipeg to look over the situation in October last, and our architect, Mr. Parkinson, drove me to four different sites. One was Grace church; another one was a block close to a newspaper building where there are some old buildings; another was across from the federal building which was built around 1934, and the other one escapes my mind. The secretary of the greater Winnipeg town planning commission spent some time with me when I was in Winnipeg. He did not come with me to visit the different sites, but I asked him if his commission had any suggestions to make and I named the different sites that I had visited. He would not commit the town planning commission. All he wanted to know was the decision of the government as to the site, so that they could continue their planning with the knowledge that we would have this new post office on a specific site. He would not tell me that the commission would take the responsibility of choosing a site; they left that to the officials of my department. He told me that when they got that information they would continue their planning, keeping in mind where the building would be erected. We have appointed real estate men as valuators in connection with one of these sites, the one across from. the newspaper building.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Across from the Winnipeg Tribune?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I think that is the one. We have people working and they
Supply-Public Works

will send in reports as to the values of these sites and then we shall expropriate or purchase by agreement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is that likely to take place soon?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If we have to proceed by expropriation, I cannot say exactly when that will be.
Do not let the speculators go to work on that property.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I think we shall have to proceed by expropriation. I find that when there are different owners and we start to purchase property prices go up, or the property changes hands and we have a lot of trouble. I believe the decision will be * to take expropriation proceedings on that block and then make offers based on the valuations handed to us by the people we have appointed. Up to now we have had no definite reports concerning the valuations. I understand that we are waiting to get the valuations from our men before taking expropriation proceedings and then we will make offers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is the minister or his department keeping in touch with the town planning commission, not because they have to, but as a matter of courtesy?

speechtext:
When we dropped the consideration of these estimates this afternoon I was about to ask the minister if he would make a statement with regard to the policy on community centres. During the war people in the various communities of Canada learned to work together much better than they had done in times of peace, or so it seemed to me. They had so many common interests, were organized for air-raid precaution work, Red Cross work and activities of one hundred and one different kinds, and as a result there developed across the country a fine community spirit. With the war over, there seems to be an eagerness to keep that spirit alive, to keep the people of the different settlements in the country working closely together. One of the main objectives is the establishment of community centres.
There are very good reasons for the establishment of such centres. The benefits are, I think, obvious to all members of the committee; they include helping the young men and women who have come back to become rehabilitated and also helping in the improvement of the health of (he people generally.
Supply-Health and Welfare

I am sure that everyone in this house during the war was shocked at the large percentage of rejections for the forces because of physical disabilities. I have not the percentage at hand at the moment, but I think it was approximately fifty per cent, in a country where standards of living are as high as anywhere else in the world. Benefits also will follow in the way of checking juvenile delinquency, which has become quite a problem throughout the country.
I thought the former Minister of National Health and Welfare, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), emphasized the importance of these centres very clearly in a statement which he made some time ago and which I will quote. He said, in a radio address:
I think one of the ways in which we can gain a new sense of cultural and social purpose after the war is through community centres. They will provide in each city and town a meeting place where all citizens can make their contribution to our social life, to art, to music, drama and sport. Community centres may very well produce more fine arts, more composers and musicians, more dramatists and actors, more poets and writers. Community centres can make a major contribution to the development of creative expression in Canada. Community centres can also, I feel, make a major contribution to the solution of the problems of adjustment that many of our service men will find on their return to civilian life.
I have learned from the minister's department that in every province there are many community centres being developed at the present time. A year or two ago there was a Gallup poll on the question, which was put to the people in the following terms:
After the war should memorials be mainly in the form of monuments, or in .the form of playing grounds, clubs, hospitals, schools and so on?
The result of the poll showed that those who wanted monuments were only ten per cent, while those who wanted useful memorials were ninety per cent. The figures for Great Britain and Australia on the same question were almost identical. In Australia, only four per cent wanted monuments and ninety-six per cent, memorials; and in Great Britain nine per cent wanted monuments and ninety-one per cent, useful memorials. So that in developing these community centres our people not only have the idea that benefits will follow, but are also building them up as memorials to our fighting men.
I want to ask the minister where the federal government fits into this picture. I suggest

to him that the very fact that these centres are designed in most cases as war memorials gives the federal government some responsibility. From my own point of view, it would have been very wise for Canada to adopt as a memorial to the fighting men of this war some such scheme rather than the beautification of the Ottawa district. I am the last one to say that the national capital should not be beautified, but I think that as a war memorial such a project is not entirely fitting. Certainly it will be of little use as a war memorial to anyone in the more distant provinces. The vast majority of such people will never even see the development and it will mean little to them. My opinion is that we would have been wiser to adopt a broad scheme of building up community centres as a war memorial.
The dominion also has a responsibility because so many veterans are involved1, and the care of the veteran is primarily the job of the dominion government. Further, I do not think there is any other way of coordinating the construction of these community centres. The cities cannot do it; the provinces cannot do it. Any effective coordination must come from the dominion, and if there is to be a national planning of such centres it must be done by the dominion.
I suggest to the minister also that the dominion might very well help in the financing of these community centres. That is done in Great Britain. I have here a booklet which the department was kind enough to lend to me. It is entitled "Community Centres", is written by John P. Kidd, and published through the agency of the Canadian council of education for citizenship. At page 79, on the subject of financing community centres in Great Britain, I find these words:
In Great Britain the ministry of education is providing grants up to 50 per cent of capital costs for new centres, and substantial grants towards extensions of present facilities.
On the following page there is some reference to what might have been done in Canada, and the extract is as follows:
At the present time, as far as is known, there is no other federal government provision for either helping to build or maintain community centres.
That is, other than wartime housing centres. Then this article goes on to say:
A deputy minister when asked what the possibilities were of such aid, stated that it was his unofficial opinion that the federal government would cooperate and share the cost with both provincial and municipal bodies, but that the initiation of individual community centres must start in the community.

Supply-Health and Welfare
That deputy minister may have been taking a good deal for granted, but I hope he was not, because he had a good idea. The suggestion has been made in British Columbia that the cost of these community centres should be split four ways, namely between the dominion, the province, the municipality and the people in the district itself. It is felt that the people in the district should accept the primary responsibility. That is essential if the community centre is to be successful. But it is also felt that the dominion should be prepared to contribute at least one-quarter of the cost.
I should like to say a word in praise of the leaders in the communities, who build up these centres. It is a difficult job and one which requires great patience, great tact and great energy. Always, where you find a good community centre you find some extremely good people behind it.
The dominion could also help by providing for the training of instructors. I find that advocated in the report of the dominion's own director of physical fitness published on April 1, 1946, where he uses these words:
It is apparent that Canada does not at present possess a sufficient number of well-trained leaders to organize an adequate physical fitness programme.
The national council on physical fitness, at their meeting in Victoria on April 5-9, 1945, had recommended as follows:
The council, recognizing the need for trained leaders, will encourage the appropriate authorities throughout the dominion to establish training courses for community leaders. By the addition of these courses to already existing ones, it is hoped that a large number of leaders will be trained this year . . .
The council endorses the principle of establishing community, recreational and cultural centres or other related recreational facilities, as war memorials.
I realize that something is being done by the council on physical fitness and by the minister's department generally to help in the training of these instructors, but there is much more to be done andi the dominion must go farther than it has already gone. Also, help could be given by the minister's department in the way of coordinating the activities in the community centres, in getting out programmes for such activities. I think the department should be represented on the various committees which are trying to build up these centres.
There may be many other ways in which the federal government could help. Probably other hon. members will have additional ideas.
In any event, I should like to have the minister tell us just what the policy of the government is with regard to these community centres. At the present time, when there is so much uncertainty as to what way of life we are to have across the world and when there seem to be different ideas in competition for men's support, I would point out that it is vitally important that we should promote all those activities which make for a fuller life in the communities across the country.

speechtext:
Before the minister replies, I should like to support the excellent presentation which has just been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Like him, I should like to express my appreciation of the work done by people in my own community- that is, in the city of Vancouver-in promoting community centres. Work done in this connection should be all the more appreciated because it is done under great financial difficulties and requires a great deal of hard, grinding effort in order to find the money to carry it on, to provide the amusements, to work out the programmes and all that sort of thing.
Last winter I was invited to a little affair arranged by one of the community centres in Vancouver, the hon. member for Vancouver South was also there. I was indeed impressed with the work they were doing. I felt guilty that I myself did not have more to do with it. There is in Vancouver an organization called the Greater Vancouver community council. Last winter this organization prepared a brief which was submitted to the federal government, I believe-very likely to the Department of National Health and Welfare -and also to the provincial governments and to the municipal authorities. The minister of education of British Columbia has gone so far as to set up a committee to investigate the need for action in this matter. This committee consists of representatives of the Vancouver school board, a representative of the city parks board, a representative of the university of British Columbia, a representative of the provincial government and a representative of the Greater Vancouver community council. The committee will note that it has widespread support throughout the community and, by virtue of the approval of the provincial government, support throughout the province. Of course anything I say in regard to this matter will, of necessity, relate to Vancouver, because that is the only part of the province I know anything about in this connection. In the brief presented by the Greater Vancouver community council to
Supply-Health and Welfare

the various governments four proposals are made which it was felt would meet the need. I will take the time of the committee to read those proposals; then they will be on record, and I think their reasonableness will appeal to hon. members. They are:
1.	The governments of the dominion of Canada and of the province of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver should financially assist in the construction and operation of community centres in approved locations in the city of Vancouver and surrounding territory.
2.	Such financial assistance should be by way of each of the two governments and the city contributing "dollar for dollar" raised by the people of the community requiring the centre- in other words each of the four parties should contribute one-quarter of the cost.
I want the committee to note that those promoting these community centres are willing to do their share by going out and raising one-quarter of whatever amount of money is required for the purpose.
3.	The board of park commissioners for Vancouver, upon whose property the approved buildings would be constructed in Vancouver, should be appointed as the administrative body for the grants and all applications would be approved as to grant, site and plans by the said board.
4.	The community associations and the parks hoard would either individually or collectively take such action as the government may deem necessary to make themselves eligible as recipients for grants from any special fund which either of the governments may have to draw upon.
I appreciate that this deals only with one small part of the community, while the hon. member for Vancouver South was urging a programme that would be applicable all across Canada. However, if this programme could be made operative in Vancouver or British Columbia, perhaps similar programmes could be made operative in other parts of the dominion. The point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, as to the federal government assisting and organizing centres of this type right across Canada is, to my mind, a timely proposal and one to which the department should give earnest consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The two hon. members from Vancouver have made the suggestion that the community or the city should do something itself. I would be remiss if I did not say that the junior chamber of commerce of Fort William went out and collected S100,000 for their community centre. If there is any hope of getting anything from the dominion government to encourage those young men we shall be glad to get it; but we have taken

the first step. Whether the dominion government does anything or not, we are going ahead anyway, because both the lakehead cities feel that this is a most important job. If you are going to reduce your police forces it will only be by taking care of your boys and girls through good clean recreation and athletics.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver South has spoken to me privately about this matter, and the hon. member for New Westminster has both spoken and written to me about it as well. I have listened with great interest to what all hon. gentlemen have had to say, and I am sure the committee will agree with the general objectives which have been outlined. There can be no doubt of the value of community centres. The experience in Britain and some of the European countries, of which I have some personal knowledge, is certainly corroborative of what has been said tonight. Likewise as an agency to control juvenile delinquency, there can be no doubt about the value of community centres, as well as for the purpose of creating general interest in what one might call the more worth-while things.
Of course I must remind the committee, and the committee will appreciate, that in this matter we can hardly compare Great Britain with our country. We are a federal state; Great Britain is a unitary state. The provinces are properly jealous of their constitutional powers. We have heard much in this house, and rightly so, of the dangers of over-centralization; and I should think if there was one field in which the community effort could best be emphasized it would be in this particular field. I believe that orderly government in this country depends largely upon the orderly working of the various jurisdictions of government, municipal, provincial and federal; and, desirable as many of these things are, one has to bear in mind constantly the division of constitutional powers. The matter is not just as easy as it has been portrayed, for in some of the provinces there is not only a jealous regard for their jurisdiction in these matters but, more than that, we have been told this is a field they regard as properly their own. It has been generally accepted, certainly up to the present time, that the basic responsibility for the development of these community centre projects belongs on the level of the provincial governments. Indeed in some provinces, certainly in one that I recall offhand, there is legislation covering this very matter;

Supply-Health and Welfare
and in one other province, where there is no legislation but some financial assistance given by some other meithod, there is a strong insistence that this is a matter coming within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and that it must be so regarded, and we in turn so regard it.
As the hon. gentleman has said, during the war in respect of wartime construction through the Wartime Housing and under my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction, certain community centres were created. That was the case in my own city; and I know of the great work and the great usefulness of those agencies from the point of view of promoting interest in art, music, the handicrafts, and so on. I can only say that in the proposals made by the dominion to the provinces at the dominion-provincial conference reference was made to the willingness of the dominion government to accept responsibility for the provision of community planning information, and to the federal government's willingness, under certain conditions, to assist the provinces and municipalities financially in the planning and carrying out of certain types of public projects. Those projects could easily come within that category; but, as my hon. friend knows, it would depend upon a pretty wide measure of agreement. However I do not think I can offer the hon. member any more encouragement, in the light of the fact that, in the nature of things, I believe the problem is essentially provincial. That is also the legal basis.
During the war, under the War Charities Act, which was administered by the Department of National War Services, and in the liquidating stages by this department, moneys were collected by various organizations, including the Canadian Legion, for the purpose of doing the very thing my hon. friend has mentioned, namely, that of creating as war memorials recreational centres, community centres and the like. Some of these funds are still in the stage of liquidation, and some have been realized. As a result, some projects have been built. I fully agree with the desirable object mentioned. Communities, such as the one to which the hon. member for Fort William has referred, can do a great deal themselves, and should be encouraged to do it, particularly in respect of purely community efforts.
I believe I can say no more to the hon. member which would be of pertinent relevance, and would only assure him that the problem is one of continuing interest.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while the national health and welfare estimates are before the house, I wish to make a few observations pertaining to the family allowances act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: First, may I emphasize once more the beneficial scope of this most important piece of social legislation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It should be pointed out, however, that most countries with a civilization comparable to our own provide legislation of this type. According to a pamphlet released before the 1945 election, family allowances have been granted in some thirty countries, and in New Zealand more particularly, for over 20 years.
In the course of my remarks, I wish to stress what I consider a gaip in the allowance act and respectfully beg the government to improve this piece of legislation at the very first opportunity. Since the end of the war, the government has had to deal with a mass
Supply-Health and Welfare

of extremely important problems entailing much lengthier sessions than those which were held formerly. For that reason, I feel it may well be excused for not yet having considered the improvements which I shall suggest and for which large families all over the country are clamouring.
I hope, however, that during the next year or two, when sessions will have resumed their normal duration, the government will find time to investigate with care the possibility of readjusting the monthly allowance grant.
The provision of the act which I now take the liberty of criticizing is that which I shall call the unexplainable decreasing rate, applied from the fifth child on.
I have not delved into the operation of family allowance legislation in other countries, but according to an article written by Father Leon Lebel, chaplain of the Catholic Farmers Union, and which appeared in the May 23, 1945 issue of Terre de chez-nous, the decreasing rate is found in no other country.
Legislators and economists of all nations agree that the first children born in any family are least in need of assistance since their parents are generally in a position to provide for them, in part, at least. In most cases, however, their means prove to be altogether inadequate from the fourth or the fifth child on.
I know that during the 1944 debates it was said that the expenses are heavier for the first children of a large family, and it is probably so, to a certain extent. That might be a sound argument if the allowances were sufficiently high to cover all the expenses incurred' in raising a child. However, that is not the purpose of the act, and nobody ever upheld the contrary. The allowances are not meant to cover all expenses, but to help needy parents. That is why, prior to January 1, 1947, people earning $3,000 did not receive any family allowances. At present, the small wage-earners benefit more from those allowances, and those earning in excess of $3,000 only draw a small measure of assistance from them.
It is therefore evident that they are meant to help those in the lower income brackets. If so, logically the allowance should be based on the parents' income and not on the expenses entailed in raising a child. In the light of that principle, which in my opinion is irrefutable, let us examine the operation of the act in its present form. The father of four children under sixteen receives the maximum amount of allowances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was saying. Mr. Chairman, that from the fifth child on, there is a monthly decrease of $1, which represents $12 a year, in the family allowance grant.
A $2 reduction applies to the sixth and seventh children, bringing the allowance down to $3 a month or $36 a year.
From the eighth child on, the monthly allowance is reduced to $2, representing a $24 yearly payment.
As I said a while ago, family allowance grants cover but a trifling part of the cost entailed by the upbringing of a child. Let us assume, by making a reasonable and generous estimate, that raising a child costs at least $100 more than the family allowance grant. In any case, allowances do not even pay for the milk which is only part of a child's diet.
It is true that, for income tax purposes, the taxpayer may deduct from his taxable income the sum of $100 for each child under 16; such a concession, however, provides no more than a $20 yearly redaction. So that for the fourth child the budget and allowances mean an aid of $80 at the most, while for the eighth child, it is less than $44.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Hon. members who very kindly requested me not to read my speech will hardly be the gainers, for I am now bound to take up twice as much time and talk forty minutes instead of twenty. But they have wished it and, since you have so ruled, Mr. Chairman, I 'shall keep up at this rate.
This decreasing rate is clearly ridiculous. No wonder it is not found in any other country. On the other hand several countries have adopted an increasing rate or its equivalent. In some countries, allowances are granted only for a second or third child, on the assumption that parents are able to support a small family. Only when they have many mouths to feed do they require government assistance. In Belgium, for instance, in addition to birth allowances, 170 francs a month are granted in respect of a first or second child, 230 francs for a third, 300 francs for a fourth, and 430 francs for a fifth or more, up to age 18.
May I quote in this connection from an article on Quebec and family allowances which appeared in the magazine America for April 13, 1946, under the signature of M. E. L. Chicanot, a Montreal publicist. This is what he writes:
Assuming that family allowances were introduced for the purpose of relieving families of the increasing burden placed upon them by the coming of each new child, and indirectly for the purpose of promoting a higher birth-rate, a particularly odd feature of this new federal legislation is the decreasing rate of the allowance.
Canada seems to be the only country, among a number who have implemented family allowance plans, where this regressive rate is in effect It is in stark contrast with the family allowances recently reintroduced in Russia, where payments start with the third child only, but progressively increase, up to the eleventh, after which they remain stationary and at a level which nevertheless appears extremely high.
The plan recently introduced in Great Britain excludes the first child and provides a weekly allowance of about $ljl2 for each additional child. Australia, which, not so long ago, raised its payments from 80 cents to around 81.20, pays that sum for each child also, from the second on.
As Canada must, in the future, rely on natural increase rather than immigration to solve her man-power problems, it is not out of reason to believe that family allowances have been devised so as to raise the birth-rate among the Anglo-Saxons, without giving undue encouragement to Quebec.
The statement that the children after the fifth cost less to bring up than the others has very little real value in the light of a somewhat realistic analysis of the situation. Here again, I refer the hon. members who desire information on the matter to the
authoritative article I mentioned a while ago, written by Rev. Father LeBel.
Thank God, there are still, in Canada, people whose lofty sentiments and Christian spirit are carried to such a degree that they do not raise any obstacle to the natural transmission of life. God be praised that there are still among us numberless people who feel that a large family is a title of nobility of which they may be justly proud. These good people, instead of being ridiculed, as often happens in certain quarters, should be brought, with due honour, to the attention of their fellow-citizens. They should be given public credit and encouraged by tangible tokens of esteem, in the form of a more generous grant on the part of the state.	.
We all know that most of the greatest figures of history belonged to large families. Unfortunately, I do not have, at hand, a complete list of these eminent personalities, but only a few notes haphazardly jotted down. In the excellent periodical Relations, Father Louis Levesque, director of the Rimouski seminary, gives us, in an article reproduced from the Centre Saint-Germain, very probant figures in connection with large families. Father Levesque points out that of forty-two seminarists attending the Rimouski seminary last year, thirty belonged to families of at least ten children. Besides, a director of a religious community, who does not identify himself, states that out of 120 youths, 79 come from families of nine children.
Finally, the director of another religious institution, the Chicoutimi seminary, I believe, points out that:
The development of vocations to the priesthood or the religious life requires favourable surroundings w-here a Christian spirit prevails. Statistics seem to prove, moreover, that, in point of fact, vocations ripen only in large families...
In another paragraph, the director states that:
In the Chicoutimi diocese, most of those who answered the calling came from large families. ... In fact, might it not be said that large families are almost the exclusive source of vocations to the priesthood and to the religious life?
Around 1930, the Saint-Vincent-de-Paul Society, while visiting needy families in Hull in order to bring them relief, made a survey of the number of children found in the assisted families. According to these figures, there were 5 families of 9 children, 6 of 7 children, 53 of one child and 52 without children; this seems to indicate that large families are not always among the poorest. This also shows that, as a general rule, virtue is rather the prerogative of large families.
Supply-Health and Welfare

Finally, here is an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press:
(Text):
Targe vs. Small Families
One of the reasons given by sociologists and economists for the smaller families of today is that many parents do not believe they can afford to rear the lusty broods which were the rule, rather than the exception, of Victorian times. Modern parents look narrowly at the costs of education and of launching their children successfully into the world.
Contrary evidence is given by an eminent savant, Professor Ernest Barker of Oxford and Cambridge.
I am not going to quote his lengthy statement hut the conclusion of the article in the Winnipeg Free Press is this:
Is it .the fact, after all, that the truly underprivileged are the children in small families?
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the house spends a great deal of time discussing immigration as a means of increasing the population of this vast country. Allow me to say that the soundest, surest and most economical way of peopling the country is to give free play to the vital forces of the nation.
We have spent millions in bringing from central Europe immigrants who, coming to Canada to amass a fortune, learned1 a useful trade among us and heaped up easily acquired capital only to return afterwards, as we saw recently, to their native country in order to further the expansion of a communist regime openly at war with our own. To my mind, we would have been wiser to assist our large families and thus prevent, to a great extent, infantile disease while checking the maternal death rate, sad factors by which in the past our people, more particularly poor families have been hard hit. In this manner, we would also have made the enjoyment of better health possible for those of our children who survived in spite of a system which was at times extremely cruel and barbarous. It is high time that we learned from the past and did everything in our power to help our citizens bear children and raise them. To my mind, it is extremely urgent to enact as soon as possible all the social legislation that was suggested at the 1945 dominion-provincial conference and has since been discussed by all our statesmen. I respectfully urge the government to introduce some legislation along those lines, even though it might not be possible to obtain the consent of all provinces. Social legislation of that kind could be of benefit to the less wealthy provinces which would see fit to take advantage of it, and some day, as happened in the case of old age pensions, the provinces will follow

suit and avail themselves of the dominion's assistance because they will be compelled to do so by public opinion within their own boundaries.
To most people the decreasing rate can only mean that it is not highly desirable that a Canadian family should have more than four children, that the government does not care to encourage overmuch the raising of large families, that the eighth child, from the standpoint of human assets, is less valuable than his elders since his allowance represents only 40 per cent of theirs.
I am conscious of the fact that the government has never intended to approach the problem in such a brutal manner. Nevertheless, such is the logical and inevitable conclusion to which the principle of a decreasing rate is leading.
The younger children of large families will not fail, as soon as they come to realize it, to resent keenly the discrimination shown against them, and in my humble opinion, it will ever rankle in their minds.
This decreasing rate has no doubt been adopted on the ground of economy. In order to ascertain what actual saving it makes possible, I have taken the trouble to make some calculations based on the figures placed on Hansard by Hon. Mr. Claxton in 1946. Now, according to those figures, the elimination of the decreasing rate would only cost this country an additional sum of six million dollars. The cost would be increased by a similar amount if a progressive rate corresponding to the present decreasing rate were put into effect. An amount of six million dollars represents but 2-3 per cent of the moneys appropriated for family allowances, and three-tenths of 1 per cent of the total expenditures of the government for 1947. In my opinion, the difference is so small that this useless provision should never have been embodied in the act, and for that reason, I wish, in concluding, respectfully to urge the government to look as soon as possible into the matter I have just raised, that is the replacement of the present decreasing rate by a corresponding progressive rate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister state the expenditure on one item to be found on page 175 of the details for professional and special services, for which a total of $300,000 was appropriated last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The expenditure was $21,902.53.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I think the answer which the minister has just given is about as significant a reflection on the way in which these estimates are made up as any that we have heard so far, and we have heard of a number of remarkable instances in the review of the estimates of this department.
This item for professional and special services, for which the government asked and received an appropriation of $300,000 last year, represented certain contemplated expenditures in connection with seeing that the family allowance was properly devoted to the purpose for which it was intended. It will be noted that the actual expenditure, out of a total of $300,000 appropriated, was $21,902.53. Let no one say that that represents an attempt at rigid economy on the part of the administration, because it does not represent that at all. What it does represent is hopelessly inaccurate budgeting, which applies to the whole basis on which the government has prepared its estimates.
The government was well warned on this subject during a discussion of this item last year. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion of this item occupied two evenings of the time of this committee. What came to our attention was this, that in the previous fiscal year 1945-46, which was not a complete year, a total of $5,995 was expended for this purpose. When we came to consider the estimate of $300,000. submitted by the predecessor of the present Minister of Health and Welfare, we found that in the two months of the fiscal year 1946-47, which had passed at the time the estimate was under review, a total of $5,000 had been spent on this item. The minister was seeking to justify an estimate of no less than $295,000 for the remaining ten months of the fiscal year, and members from all parties sitting in opposition in this house rose and expressed themselves in quite strong terms about an item which had so little in fact to justify so large an amount asked for by the government. I remember undertaking to make a suggestion as to what actually was
justified on the strength of the information given to the house, and I will take the liberty of referring to the statement as recorded in Hansard, because the predecessor of the present minister took me to task for presuming to offer so low a calculation of what would be justified in this particular item. At pages 3009 and 3010 of Hansard of last year, I am reported as having said:
May I say with all possible emphasis that the case made out today in substantiation of an estimate of $300,000 is a ease which, on examination, will not justify the expenditure of more than $25,000 or $50,000.
The minister then followed and put on a great show of indignation at the idea of having so small an amount offered in lieu of the $300,000 which he was asking from the house, and he said, as reported at page 3010 of Hansard:
To set down a lesser sum than $300,000 would be misleading.
After twelve months of the fiscal year in operation, we find that a total of $21,902 was expended, so that even I was too high in my estimate of $25,000. I do not hold the present minister personally responsible for what, I think, was an imposition perpetrated by his predecessor on the committee of the whole in respect of this item, but I do say that the whole government shares the collective responsibility for perpetrating an imposition of that kind on the committee, and it leaves us all, I believe, feeling that we cannot approach the consideration of the estimates of the government with any degree of confidence at all when we find such a hopelessly inaccurate budgeting going on as is illustrated in this item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is the minister going to reply to the hon. gentleman before I speak?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I have already replied to the hon. member. I am mot criticizing him for making t'he observations he has. He has made them several times during the estimates and I am not criticizing him for doing so. I can only say in reply that my predecessor, whose magnificient contribution to this department is one that is well recognized, was naturally placed in a difficult position, with regard to this major division of the department. With no experience on which to rely, where his estimates had to be necessarily based on conjecture, it is no faulty admission to say that the estimates in this particular instance were greatly exaggerated. It does not mean, however, that the money was wastefully spent, because to the extent of the extent of the excess there was no expenditure. It was an overestimate, and' was partly extenuated, how-
Supply-Health and Welfare

ever, by the fact that agreements with certain provinces in respect of projected investigational work were not completed.
The estimate this year has been reduced by $150,000, and I have no doubt that I shall be placed in the position either of having underestimated this time or of having overestimated to some extent. It simply is not possible to calculate to the mathematical degree of accuracy on. which the hon. gentleman seems to insist. I can only say that experience is a great teacher, and in this new department, which is doing an extremely important welfare job from day to day, we are learning how to improve our methods and, I trust, our calculations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I follow up the minister's remarks with this observation. do it when I have finished. speechtext:
In Nova Scotia we have
an agreement. The current monthly rate is $1,050. The total estimate is $12,600. Administration cases, fees paid to individuals or agencies for handling trust accounts of families when the allowance has to be taken from the parent and turned over to a trustee for administration; the yearly administration fee is $20 per case, totalling about 500, or an estimate of $10,000.
