maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to refer to the subject of agreements with the provinces respecting various investigational work on family allowances, and to ask the minister whether it would be possible to go farther along those lines and have the provinces do more of the work in the administration of family allowances. I asked a question to that effect on February 24, as reported on page 707 of Hansard of this year, as follows:
Was any attempt made to have the provinces administer family allowances, or make family allowances payments, through their existing provincial public and private welfare agencies?
The answer to that question was no, and the reasons were given in a subsequent paragraph of the answer to the effect that the Family Allowances Act itself provided for



Supply-Health and Weljare
the Department of National Health and Welfare to have sole responsibility for and charge over the administration of the act. I asked further questions as to the cost by provinces of administering family allowances. In a return dated February 27, the information was provided for the three years, 1945-46, 1946-47 and an estimate for the year 1947-48. The round figures for 1946-47 showed the total cost to the dominion government of administering family allowances to be 83,737,169; and it is estimated that in the next year that cost will rise to 83,881,415, or a total of nearly $4,000,000.
There are, I think, several considerations which were urged that, so far as possible, the administration of family allowances be decentralized by virtue of agreements made with the provinces. In the first place, of course, they already have existing social services, the provincial governments' social and welfare agencies. In addition, there are numerous private welfare and social agencies already in the field, who have accumulated a great deal of experience, both administrative and theoretical. It seems to me that these services could do the job, I will not say more efficiently, but certainly more efficiently at first, because they have the experience. Moreover, if they were used it would not be necessary for the dominion government to set up a complete staff of its own, so that duplication could be avoided. In the second place, if one reads the annual report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1946, reference will be found to the reason it was necessary to increase the staff. Regional directors had to be appointed for a number of the provinces. A further difficulty was found in getting accommodation. I should like to refer to the report itself, at page 77:
As at the end of the fiscal year, accommodation in Toronto and Halifax was however still unsuitable, and efforts were being continued by the Department of Public Works to obtain better space.
There you have proof that the question of accommodation is costing the dominion government some money as well as some effort; and with the shortage of accommodation that exists at the moment, on its face it would appear to be inefficient for the federal government to set up its own staff, requiring an expenditure for their salaries as well as for office accommodation and the paying of rent, or the construction of further buildings. This also complicates the position as far as the provincial government agencies are concerned, because they are also short of office space, for which the dominion is now in competition with them.

Finally, as the minister himself has mentioned, agreements have been completed with the provinces for carrying out the investigational work. That is referred to at page 79 , of the report. It appears that more provinces are being brought under the terms of these agreements; and if that can be done in this respect it seems to me that the possibility at least should be explored as to whether the provinces would be willing to carry out some of this work under the dominion department in so far as the administration and investigation of family allowance benefits are concerned. The fact is that some $4,000,000 is expended on administration costs alone; and while I am not saying that is too much, I am suggesting that it could be reduced by decentralizing the work in the provinces, and carrying it on in a more efficient manner. Would the minister care to comment on these suggestions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in saying, at the outset, that parliament has correctly decided that the administration shall rest with the body which pays out the money.
I think that is a sound principle, and I know of no reason to suggest that we should change it. I believe it is wise to do what we are doing. I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate that the cost of family allowances has been remarkably low, when one considers that it represents about T6 per cent of the total expenditure. I think the committee has every reason to be pleased with the administration of family allowances by this government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Because of the very low cost. The figure 1-6 represents the cost, not only to this department, but to public works and finance as well. One-quarter of the cost is taken up by postage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Would the minister give
the figures?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Our own actual cost in the department is 0-8 per cent, and I feel that these figures should commend themselves to hon. gentlemen.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In the course of my remarks I said I was not trying to suggest that the department was being inefficient or extravagant in its administration. My suggestion was that a change in the set-up might lower the cost; and the fact that it is already low does not alter the fact that it is costing nearly $4,000,000. If we could save only $2,000,000 of that I should think it would be well worth while. Admittedly, parliament passed the act and gave the

Supply-Health and Welfare
sole responsibility to the federal government; but on a reading of the debate at that time it is not easy to discover that any great consideration was given to the question I am now bringing forward. In this connection, as well as others, it seems to me that the administration as well as the investigational work should be left to the agency closest to the people concerned, which is certainly the municipal and provincial governments. I do not think it is any answer to say we are doing it for only $4,000,000 now, or S3,800,000. The committee should be shown whether it would be less expensive to do it in any other way. If it would be less expensive, then I think it should be done in that other way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I had some critical remarks to make of the Department of National Health and Welfare, but at this stage I might tell the minister this legislation is very popular with the people in all parts of Canada, certainly with those in my part of the country. Since the act was passed, I have had only two letters in connection with family allowance problems. In one case the parents had failed to register the births of their children, and I shall refer to the second case in just a moment. Only today I had personal proof of the efficiency of this department. It is not yet a month since our older daughter became sixteen; yet when the cheque arrived at home today it was S8 less than formerly. I was hoping that there might have been a mistake in attending to these matters, Sut when they are adjusted so quickly, and when hon. members have had so few complaints, I gather that this is an efficiently operated branch.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You would not have taken the money, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It would work just as quickly the other way if you should have another child.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have a letter from the Canadian Legion at ICelvington, Saskatchewan, concerning a case I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The secretary of the branch writes as follows:
The above-named was married in England during the year 1043 and his wife arrived in Canada about a year ago. At the time of the marriage Mrs. - had two sons ages five and eleven years and the sons remained in the family and came over to Canada last year. Application was made for family allowance on behalf of these children but same was refused apparently under section 2 of the Family Allowance Act which requires three years residence in Canada before being registered.
I find that section 2 makes provision for children who are born while the father or 83166-285J
mother was a member of the naval, military or air forces of Canada, or within twelve months after the father or mother ceased to be a member of the forces. It is obvious that when the act was passed we did not have in mind cases such as these. The secretary of the legion goes on to say:
The position is that these children had received dependants' allowances from the Canadian government during residence in England after the marriage of the veteran and it was no fault of theirs that they were not in Canada immediately after marriage and in this manner establish the residence to qualify. It appears to me that the children would be discriminated against as compared with Canadian children if they do not receive the allowance and it is hard to believe that stepchildren acquired by a soldier by marriage overseas should not be considered Canadian children, especially when they were unable to come to this country until after the war was over.
I wrote the minister in connection with this case about a month and a half ago, but he has not had an opportunity to reply. I do not imagine there are many in this category, but it seemed to me that the Canadian Legion made a reasonable request when they asked that children in this category should be eligible for the benefits of family allowances. Could the minister make a statement?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have had similar letters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are few cases in this category; I think it is a diminishing problem. I understand that the children to whom the hon. gentleman refers were born in England of English parents; is that right?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

This is a matter very
close to my heart. The hon. gentleman will recall that one of the dominion government's proposals had to do with crippled children and handicapped persons. In the Department of Veterans Affairs some considerable work so far as veterans is concerned has been done under a gentleman who is himself handicapped, a gallant soldier, Major Dunlop. I am very happy to make reference to Major Dunlop whom I have known since I was a young lad. Then in the Department of Labour work in connection with the handicapped is being prosecuted with serious attention by Mr. Hudson under the present Minister of Labour.
With regard to the study referred to by my hon. friend, I have established in my department a sort of seminar to review this problem, and we have been reviewing it now for several months in order to get a proper perspective of the matter in all its implications and it has wide implications. Major Dunlop, Mr. Hudson and others from the national welfare council have been sitting in and giving us the benefit of their views on this matter.
My hon. friend will understand that a system of disability benefits depends in many ways upon and is attached to pensions for the aged, unemployment insurance and particularly health insurance. a result of persuasion by the provincial authorities, Mr. Hudson and Major Dunlop. The suggestion was made that they take these people on. Every hon. member knows of hundreds of cases of people in need through no fault of their own. There are many women who stay at home to take care of an aged mother or some other member of the family and who later find themselves deprived of the ability to earn a living. When I was home at Easter I was talking to a woman who had taken care of her father who was in receipt of a pension. The father died; the pension stopped, and this woman who does not know how to do anything else is just as helpless as a person of sixty-five or seventy years. Many times the situation is complicated by ill health. 21,1. Victorian Order of Nurses, $13,100.

When this item was up last session and the session before, when the estimates of the previous minister were under consideration, I had something to say about the Victorian Order of Nurses, and I urged the then minister to consider the question of increasing the amount for the national office of this worthy organization. The Victorian Order provides a service for all, regardless of race, creed or financial status, and meets the needs of those patients who cannot afford a nursing service. There are 103 branches scattered across the country, and the order is supported by fees from patients, fees from insurance companies for service to policy holders, and municipality and township grants, and from additional moneymaking efforts on the part of local boards. The national office
[Mr Fleming.]
is also supported by government grants, interest on endowment funds and subscriptions.
The service has so expanded over the last few years that the national office finds itself in an embarrassing' position. According to the last financial statement, the following deficits were recorded:	in 1944, a deficit of
$12,772.12; in 1945, a deficit of $42,575.38; and in 1946, a deficit of $46,576.27. This is not a very comforting position. These deficits have had to be covered by expenditure of capital, thus depleting one of the main sources of operating revenue.
There are some 450 nurses, and of the 103 branches, twenty-nine have been organized during the last ten years since this grant was given in 1934. The number of patients served during 1945 was 100,118; the number of visits made during the'same year was 756,984. Of these, fifty per cent were free and eighteen per cent partly paid. The federal grant of 813,100 per annum was first set up in 1934. But since that grant was set up, the services have increased by same thirty-eight or thirty-nine per cent, in the last ten years. Revenues have been consistently reduced by declining interest rates and more especially by depletion of capital funds to cover operating deficits. Expenses have increased sharply with expansion of service, and it has been necessary, since 1934, to offer scholarships and1 uniform allowances totalling in excess of $70,000 to attempt to maintain and build up a force of skilled public health nurses to ensure an efficient and adequate nursing service throughout Canada.
I am not too familiar with the background of this grant of $13,100 set up in the estimates, but if it was considered in 1934 to be a fair grant, then certainly a greater amount should be granted today, having regard to the increased services rendered and the increased costs of operation. The national office has increased its activities through the expansion of the order to such an extent that, as I have intimated, it is going behind every year. Through the necessity of expanding the services, increased expenditures have been necessary to get the properly trained nurses. This amount should be greatly increased.
Before taking my seat, I should like to pay tribute to a great Canadian woman in the person of Miss Elizabeth Smellie, C.B.E., who for many years served as chief superintendent of the Victorian Order of Nurses, and was wartime leader of the Canadian army nursing services. It is doubtful if any Canadian woman, contemporary or otherwise, has contributed more to her country and whose name and record are of more national renown.

A month ago, at the Prime Minister's request, I was asked to attend a function in her honour, and on behalf of the government and the people of Canada to pay a tribute to Miss Smellie who had completed twenty-five years of great work in that organization. As Minister of National Health and Welfare, it is only proper that I should pay tribute to the untiring efforts of a great Canadian woman, who has achieved so much.
The grant to this organization in the period 1914-15 to 1922-23 was S5,000; from 1923-24 to 1931-32 the grant was $10,000. In the period 1923 to 1934 the grant was reduced to $9,000; and in 1935, a significant date, it was increased to $13,100.
On what basis was that increase made? Why was it set at that figure?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I was not in office then. My hon. friends were. I do not really want to put it in that way. We were not in office at that time, and I could hardly be held accountable for the policy of another government, representing another political party. But I suppose it was because those were difficult days when reductions in expenditure were the order of the day. I suppose it was part of the then government's policy to curtail. I can offer no other reason.
The amount was set in 1935. The minister's administration set that $13,100, and my question is this: why was it set at that figure at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I suppose it was because that was conceived to be the extent to which the administration was prepared to go with regard to assistance. It represented a considerable increase, and I suppose every $100 would count.
Was it because of the size of the order or the amount of money they required each year; that is, the amount of their budget for the year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No. It was the figure set.
In other words, the minister has not that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I cannot say why it was $13,100, but I suppose the minister of the day
who made representations to his colleagues determined, in the light of all other grants, that it was a fair amount to give.

Then, owing to the
increased services which are being rendered today, I would urge that the minister take into serious consideration helping this worthy order in proportion to the increase in their activities. I do not ask that he do it now, but, say in the next year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I shall be glad to give serious consideration to that.
How is this $13,100 apportioned or expended?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is given to the national office.
It is just given direct to the national office?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.

That is not a very satisfactory answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Well, I am no seer. It look as though this item will be liquidated this year, but I want to give an honest answer and that is the only answer any honest man can give. In regard to the grants to the nurses' association, the amount estimated last year was $25,535-
No, I am speaking of the total; I need not trouble the minister for the details. What was the total expenditure corresponding with the estimate last year of $10,158,760?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The expenditure was $283,064,172; and unliquidated, $47,525.58.

The minister is on the wrong question. He has gone back to something I asked a. short time ago. The present question is, what was the total expenditure in 1946-47 corresponding to the total estimated expenditure on page 74 of the estimates, which is given as $10,158,760?

This year you are estimating the expenditure of $390,000, which actually is an increase of about $100,000, not a decrease.

speechtext: I did not hear one word you said; I am sorry.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

How far back must I go? This reminds me of a long-distance telephone conversation where you find, half-way through your conversation, that the line has been cut.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: 279. Departmental administration, $227,019.

Mr. Chairman, living as I do in Halifax, a long distance from Ottawa, I generally have to stay here most of the time. In view of the fact, however, that in the near future an event is to take place in Halifax, I may have to travel home more frequently. Before doing so, I should like to take this opportunity to say a few words with respect to public works.
You should get home in time to vote, at any rate.

With that in mind, I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works various projects which I have placed before him from time to time, because I believe they are important not only to Halifax but to the fishing industry of Nova Scotia. I refer to such items as breakwaters, wharves and causeways which affect the work of fishermen in our province. I do not expect a complete answer this evening, but I would ask his officials to give these items the careful consideration which I believe they deserve.

Will the hon. member
include the Halifax-Dartmouth tunnel?

I have listened to the hon. member for Royal on more than one occasion interrupt me when I have been speaking about matters relating to Halifax, concerning which he has shown very little knowledge. On this occasion I do not propose to deal with such interruptions.

I have a pretty clear
knowledge as to why these items are to be discussed now.
I have no intention of entering into any controversy on any foolish subject which might be raised in an effort to draw me away from what I have in mind.
Save it for the hustings.
I have brought the attention of the Minister of Public Works to projects which we really require.
You have needed them for a long time.
As I said before, I do not mention these matters because of the event hon. members opposite have in mind. I have discussed them repeatedly.
And you have got nowhere with them.

I have been successful in getting a number of them, but naturally there are others which are just as urgent. First, I shall draw the minister's attention to the very important item of dredging. One cannot very well sail in or out of some of these fishing coves without the proper depth of water. From time to time they fill up and require dredging. I have in mind, first, Herring Cove, a well known fishing district in Halifax county. Then, on more than one occasion I have brought Eastern Passage to the minister's attention. It has been slowly losing its fishing industry because the fishermen cannot leave or enter that point with the degree of safety which is required. Then, I would mention Paul's Point, another well known fishing centre; and also the beautiful spot with the lovely name of Modesty Cove.
Did you say "honesty"?
I could take hon. members to that point and they would agree with me as to its beauty. They would, I am sure, join with me in urging that my request be given every consideration.

Is this a list of deficiencies of the government?

Supply-Public Works

The hon. member made his speech in Halifax a few nights ago. While he must realize it was not well received, still I hope he enjoyed his trip to Halifax and will come back again some time after July 14. It may do him no harm, and we will try to make his return visit as interesting as we did the last one.
On a point of order, do we not discuss dredging under item 306?

I know the hon. member does not want to be too careful about these items. We are dealing with administration and you cannot carry out any particular item without the proper administration. Therefore I feel quite justified in dealing with this and other matters.
The second matter I wish to deal with is the need of breakwaters. This is closely connected with the fishing industry, because you cannot give the fishermen in these fishing communities protection for their boats without breakwaters.
Did the hon. member say "votes" or "boats".
Boats.
He said fishing for votes.
For fish or suckers.

The hon. member of the official opposition made a kindly reference, not at all like the one just used by the other hon. member.
In connection with breakwaters, I am going to refer to some definite places. Ketch Harbour is a well known fishing district and a breakwater is required there. One is required also at Little Harbour and also at Portuguese Cove. Then I would mention Upper Prospect, Mosher Cove, Smiley's Point, Herring Cove, Meagher's Point and Paul's Point.
Are those places all in the county of Halifax?

A breakwater is also required at Devil's Island. I should like to deal in more particular with Devil's Island. I do not propose to go over it fully again, but previously I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. On August 10, 1946, I referred at some length to Devil's Island and the need of the inhabitants for protection. As I pointed out, it is almost impossible to leave the island at times without this protection and they have been unable to procure medical aid when it was badly needed. I want the minister to bear this Devil's Island project in mind and perhaps he will tell me what has been done in the way of surveys and1 so on.
A large number of wharf repairs are required and it is readily understood why these repairs are needed at the present time. During the war we were told that economy was the policy and the necessary repairs were not carried out to a number of these wharves. I would mention Baker's Point, Dover East, Dover West, Owl's Head, Ship Harbour, Upper Prospect, Shad Bay, Ostrea Lake and Ketch Harbour.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do not miss any coves.
That is a short list but they are all fishing villages. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and those who come from inland places are not familiar with the needs of these fishermen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Four generations on that coast; I know all about it.
On a point of order, I should like to ask whether these matters should not be discussed on the estimates of the chief electoral officer rather than those of the Department of Public Works?
I am afraid I shall have to call to my assistance the hon. member for Vancouver North to administer another spanking to the hon. member for Kamloops if he interrupts again in such a foolish manner.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The last spanking was effective for a while.
Once again I want to carry on with the fishing industry.
Oh, oh.

What are you fishing for,
Suckers?
The season will be over on July 14.

My hon. friend asks if I am fishing for suckers. I want to tell him that we do not deal with that sort of thing in our fishing villages; we throw back the suckers, as we have no use for them. If the hon. member will come down to Halifax some time I will take him out through the fishing districts, and if he uses that sort of language he will not be welcome.
There is one piece of causeway construction which I am under the impression has been started already, but I want to make sure it will be carried through to completion. I refer to the causeway at Three Fathoms harbour. This is not the causeway in Halifax harbour referred to a little while ago by the hon. member for Royal. Then there are a few skidways required. These do not cost very much money and I know they will be con-
Supply-Public Works

structed if I just bring them to the attention of the minister. One is needed at Duncan's Cove and one at Bald Rock.
There is one important matter I should like to refer to which was brought up a year or so ago in connection with the R.M.S. Queen Elizabeth and the reason why she left Halifax to sail to New York. Having the fine harbour that we have, I never could understand why it was necessary for the Queen Elizabeth to leave Halifax and turn toward New York. The reason given was that a southeast wind would endanger the ship. We never ask for anything in the way of dredging, but we do require a permanent breakwater at Mauger's Beach to provide the necessary protection from southeast winds. If the minister will be good enough to give us that breakwater we shall have without question the safest and finest harbour in North America and perhaps in the whole world.
It is just the Atlantic coast you are dealing with.
I will leave it to my hon. friend to deal with the Pacific coast. I doubt very much if the Queen Elizabeth could enter Vancouver harbour. Just think that over.
She could get into Nanaimo all right.

In connection with this breakwater at Mauger's Beach I remember receiving letters from the minister in February and March in which he stated that borings would be commenced in May. We are now into June and I should like to know if those borings have been commenced.
Was that back in the cold weather?

I ask the minister to make a note of that and let me know whether those borings have been started.
Now to satisfy the hon. member for Royal in regard to the Halifax-Dartmouth bridge, I hesitate to mention this because it might be said that I have an election in mind. If there is one thing I would not want the committee to think it is that such a thing is in my mind at the present time. However I do remember sitting in the Halifax forum in 1930 and seeing a large banner right across the back of the platform reading, "Elect R. B. Bennett and he will give you the Halifax-Dartmouth bridge." Mr. Bennett was speaking in Halifax at that time and he made that definite promise. I never make that kind of promise, but I do make strong appeals to the government of the day to do certain things. I do not make promises
You are not a leader yet. .

And. I am not likely to be, nor am I anxious to resume that responsibility, recognizing my shortcomings, but I am always ready to offer constructive thoughts, and I am asking the Minister of Public Works to consider the possibility of cooperating, with the provincial government, the city of Halifax and the town of Dartmouth in regard to building a Halifax-Dartmouth bridge. I have written the deputy minister of public works in regard to the construction at Vancouver of the Second Narrows bridge, to which a federal contribution was made on June 24, 1925, and a further payment later. In all, the total commitment in connection with this bridge was $269,936. If that can be done on the west coast, are we not as good as the east coast? We feel that if it. was found possible to help construct the Second Narrows bridge at Vancouver the department could assist in the construction of a similar bridge to connect Halifax and the enterprising town of Dartmouth on the east side of the harbour.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, in view of the remarks of the hon. member I just wish to point out to you that we on this side will expect to have the advantage of a general discussion on this item.

I do not see any point of order in that, but I do not mind an interruption of that kind..
I should not like to resume my seat without extending thanks to the Minister of Public Works for some of the projects which he has carried out at Halifax during the past year.
Let us have a list of them.

I shall be glad to comply with the request of the hon. member and mention a few of them. I thank the Minister of Public Works for the sub-post office in Halifax North, an item for which is included in these estimates. We have been working for years for a sub-post office in Halifax North, which is one of the most important sections of the city of Halifax. I hope that the post office will be started this year.
If it took many years to get this post office, how long will it take to get all the other things for which the hon. member is asking?
I hope this will be started within the next three months.
What does the minister say?

I hope he will say that we can look forward to having the work started within

Supply-Public Works
the next two or three months. If he says that he will carry it out; I know him well enough to believe he will do so. I would also thank him for the item in his estimates for the Halifax Armdiale post office. That is also a sub-post office which is badly required in a very fine and growing district. Many hon. members know the district and I know it will serve the people in a proper manner.
While credit should go to the Department of Veterans Affairs, I want to thank the Minister of Public Works because his department is looking, after the construction of the addition to Camp Hill hospital, to look after the needs of our ex-service men.
Why not have a record made and sent down there?
The hon. member was down . there and perhaps he left a record.
It was the most hospitable place I was ever in.

That is the way we teach them to be down there. Through cooperation, we extend a welcome to all who visit Halifax.
Just one other thought in closing. I wish to refer to the retirement age of casual employees such as labourers, sweepers and helpers. You retire them at sixty-five as though they were enjoying civil service superannuation or a pension. These men are not particularly fitted for all types of work, but they can carry on their present work beyond the age of sixty-five in an efficient manner.
It is the only kind of work they can do, and until such time as we bring in an old age pension bill to provide for that class of men at sixty-five, I believe that the department- and this applies to all departments-should permit these men to carry on their work at least until they are seventy years of age.
I wish to thank the minister and the members for allowing me to outline a few of the needs of my constituency, and I know I shall have the cooperation of all members in pressing the minister to provide these works at as early a date as possible.

I would ask the minister to have an investigation made of the heavy damages done by the floods at Toronto island to the breakwater. Many stores and houses, roads and yards were flooded. A return was ordered yesterday about this matter. Would the minister order a complete report on the federal breakwater at Wards, at Centre island and Gibraltar point on lake Ontario, and also answer the questions I raised just before six o'clock in regard to the parliament grounds,
monuments and traffic here, and better care of the monuments and parking cars on roadways.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
If I recall what the hon. member said just before six o'clock he wanted me to undertake to move the monuments around the parliament buildings. We have no jurisdiction to do that. The grounds are under the care of the federal district commission, and I dare not touch those monuments or try to move them around.
As to the damage caused by floods at Toronto, after the hon. member came to see me I gave instructions to our engineer, Mr. Wilson, in Toronto, to make a survey of the breakwater and to report on any damage that took place there, and if this work comes under the jurisdiction of my department it will receive our best attention.
This afternoon the hon. member spoke about the circulation on parliament hill. The other day in answer to a question in the house I mentioned that some doubts had arisen about our jurisdiction under the act of 1931 concerning circulation on government properties. The act has been submitted to the justice department for their opinion, and if they find that we have not the necessary authority under the act we will certainly, not this session, but at another session, have an amendment made to the act.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Halifax for having begun his speech by stating that he would not ask me for definite answers to all the requests he had made. Indeed, I would be at a loss to make a definite statement with reference to each of these projects. The officials will have Hansard tomorrow or next week, and, as they do for every other member, they will give careful attention to any request made by the hon. member for Halifax.
This must be the first time that he has brought them forward.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No; he has spoken to me about different projects before. I have received several visits from members on both sides of the house, and I try to be courteous and polite when they come to see me. I give instructions to my officials to do their best to give any help they can. I should like to add one more word in regard *to Halifax. Last year, during the debate on my estimates, a question arose about the breakwater or wharf at De\ il's island.

Protection work.
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Protection work at Devil's Island. Perhaps I was a little tired of the discussion and cut it rather short, but the hon. member for Halifax was kind enough to send me a book entitled "We Keep this Light," by Madame Richardson. He sent this to me after the session and I had much pleasure in reading it. I am interested in Devil's Island, but there are few people living there and the expenditure is so great that my officials hesitate before committing the department to the spending of such large amounts of money. However, the hon. member may rest assured that the request from Halifax will receive serious consideration, and I may say the same with reference to the request from any other member.
There is always a general discussion on the first item of a department on going into supply, namely, administration, and I agree that it is a good thing to have members state everything they wish to either in praise of the estimates or in criticism. But I suggest that if any hon. member wishes to discuss a specific item the proper procedure would be to wait until that item is called. I have no objection to a general discussion, but if anyone wishes to discuss breakwaters or public buildings I suggest that he should wait until the appropriate item comes up for discussion. That is the proper way to proceed.

The city of Toronto gets nothing, whatever, and yet it is the chief taxpaying city in the Dominion of Canada; there is hardly a dollar in the estimates of the Public Works Department for that city. We spent over $30 million of our civic money on Toronto harbour and grade separation. That is the only harbour in Canada on which there are two representatives of the government. There are three representatives of the city, and all the money spent by the harbour board is civic money, chargeable to real estate and paid for by the taxpayers of that city. I am very much worried as one of the representatives from that city. We have one post office from which the government gets $13 million. There is a federal breakwater at Toronto island for which the dominion government has accepted responsibility since confederation, but little money has been spent on it over the past thirty years. There are some 20,000 people living on the island in the summer and fewer in the winter, and it is in a deplorable condition. It is now flooded. Many people have lived there all winter in view of the shortage in city accommodation. There is one boat crossing the bay and it has to break the ice in the winter time. The cottages are now under water; the whole island

is ruined by the flood, and the time has come for this government to send someone there and to announce a definite policy in connection with that island. The minister, I may say, came to our city on one occasion and we were glad to entertain him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: More than once.

He was properly tendered a dinner and a luncheon by the city and the harbour board, and altogether he had a pleasant visit. I wish you had been there also, Mr. Chairman. He was out on the new harbour boat and inspected the harbour, and I do not think I am revealing any secrets when I say that we took him to Woodbine where he placed a few small bets, so that it was a profitable and enjoyable trip for him. I can assure him that a similar warm welcome awaits him the next time he comes. Whether he will do anything for us or not is another matter.
However, the other day I went over to the island and I saw for myself the condition there. I saw water on the main street and thousands of men, women and children have to live under those conditions. Some have to wear their top boots in water and all that sort of thing. One fellow selling bread had a hard time of it. The bread was all covered with water. The city has contributed nearly one-third of all income taxes received in the dominion, and I think it should get something in return. We have had no representative from the Toronto district in the federal cabinet since 1Q3S, whereas we used to have four or five members in the cabinet. No wonder we do not get anything. Of course, to the victor belong the spoils, especially in this department, where it seems that has been the policy by all parties for many years past.
We did have a harbour board, and the city contributes a large part of the cost of reclaiming and rebuilding the waterfront. It bought it out and spent a large sum of money on the harbour and island. People can go to the island for the price of a streetcar ticket and it is the working man's summer resort. I hope the minister will visit the city again and look over that district.
The courts, I may say, are without space. The city bought 465 Bay street, the dominion building. The city hall is overcrowded, and the city bought this dominion building across the road. I urge upon the minister the importance of looking into this matter. It may not be in his department, and of course I appreciate the fact that he has a hard time in finding space. I do not want to worry him, but I think he should come to the city of Toronto and witness fc-r himself the result the terrible storms have had on the island.

Supply-Public Works

I wish I were in the position of the hon. member for Halifax and could give thanks to the minister for having done something for my constituency and my province last year and for having made provision this year, but I am afraid my remarks will be critical because of the apparent discrimination in the distribution of the moneys to be voted for public works. The committee will note that there is a total of approximately $46 million to be voted to the minister's department, and about one-quarter of this is to be spent in the city of Ottawa. About half of the money is to be spent on two items, one classified as construction, repairs and improvement to public buildings, and the other as construction, repairs and improvements to harbours and rivers. In connection with these two items, the estimates are broken down into provinces, and I have taken the trouble of adding them up to show the committee just how this money, approximately half of the vote, is spent.
In connection with improvements to public buildings, Nova Scotia gets $112,500, and all this, by the way, is to be spent in Halifax. New Brunswick gets $131,000, and Prince Edward Island gets $50,000. Then there is another item of $200,000 to be divided between the three maritime provinces. So I have divided this $200,000 equally among those three provinces, and I find that Nova Scotia is to get $178,500; New Brunswick, $197,000, and Prince Edward1 Island, $116,000.
What do the farmers in the west get for wheat?

I am coming to that. Now we come to the province of Quebec. They get $2,436,650. The province of Ontario gets $2,574,000. The province of Manitoba gets $403,000. The province of Saskatchewan gets $179,500. The province of Alberta gets $667,200, and the province of British Columbia gets $963,400.
When we come to the provision for harbours and rivers we find that Nova Scotia gets $4,716,600, out of a total of $4,895,100 for harbours, rivers and public buildings. For expenditure on rivers and harbours, New Brunswick gets $767,000, or a total, including expenditure on public buildings, of $964,600. Prince Edward Island gets an expenditure for harbours and rivers of $415,500, or a total expenditure of $531,500. Quebec gets, with respect to harbours and rivers, $3,556,500, or a total expenditure of $5,993,150 for public works in Quebec. Ontario gets, with respect to harbours and rivers, $4,017,000, or a total of public works expenditures of $6,591,000. Manitoba gets, with respect to harbours and
rivers, $536,500, or a total expenditure on public works of $939,500. Saskatchewan and Alberta are lumped together with regard to harbours and rivers and they get $25,000 together. Saskatchewan gets an improvement of $70,000 at Waskesiu lake in the Prince Albert national park. So Saskatchewan will get in that respect $82,500, or a total expenditure of $262,000 for public works in that province for the coming year. Alberta gets only the $12,500 as far as rivers and harbour installations are concerned, or a total expenditure of $679,700. British Columbia's expenditure on harbours and rivers is $2,006,000, or a total expenditure of $2,969,400 on public works.
Not nearly enough.

Possibly it is not enough, but I should like the committee to consider the discrimination against the three western provinces and especially as against the province of Saskatchewan which gets a total expenditure of $262,000.
What are you going to use it for?

We will not enter into a debate on that just at the present time. I submit that in the province of Saskatchewan we have as many requests for public buildings and other things as hon. members have in any other province in Canada. I submit that this is discrimination and that it should not happen again. I looked up last year's estimates and the same thing happened then; it also happened the year before, I believe. I think the three western provinces are being discriminated against, and I protest.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Just a minute, Mr. Chairman.; I cannot allow that statement to go unchallenged. The hon. member mentioned the figures for harbours and rivers for every province. Would he be ready to admit that in his province of Saskatchewan, or in Alberta, there is no seaside and there are no ports or large rivers where there is navigation?
Yes, I admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Under these
items we try to help along the seaboard at both coasts, on the St. Lawrence and on the great lakes. The hon. member says we spent more in Nova Scotia. That has been going on for years and there is a good reason for it. There is more coastline along the Nova Scotia
Supply-Public Works

seaboard than in any other province in the dominion. Furthermore, in Nova Scotia more people depend for their livelihood on harbour facilities than in any other province in Canada. That is the explanation. No grain grower would think of dredging out in Manitoba except in lake Winnipeg. I will call as a witness one of my hon. friend's own colleagues, the hon. member for Selkirk, and ask him if we are not taking care of works which are needed to help the people out there? I like hon. members to be fair and not lead the country to believe that we are spending all our money in Nova Scotia and not spending money on dredging or building breakwaters or wharves in Saskatchewan. Where would we do it?
That is why I divided the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Yes, you divided them and then you added.

What about public
buildings?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Compare public buildings with some other province. The hon. member himself says that we have an estimate of only some $112,000 for the whole province, and that we have some $4 million odd for rivers and harbours to help the fishermen who are creating new wealth, just as we try to help the grain growers out west. That is the whole policy. It is the policy not only of this government, but has been the policy of every government since confederation. Those who have experience in these matters will support what I am saying tonight. Does the hon. member think it is fair to go out to Manitoba or to his province and say, "Now, listen, New Brunswick receives $765,000 for harbours-
For public buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Let us see what they have for public buildings right in this.
Look at Quebec and Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
If you give me time I will give you an explanation for Ottawa. You say that half of the money is spent in Ottawa. It cannot be spent elsewhere. That is where we have our activities. We take care of all the public buildings the government needs for its some twenty odd departments. The government here needs a staff. The hon. member is complaining that the buildings are not well maintained or in a good state of repair. He will admit that right in the city of Ottawa we have 150 buildings or thereabouts owned or occupied by the government.

I will just try to put the hon. gentleman right. I try to be fair, but, really, the remarks he made tonight are of a kind that I have not heard in the last seventeen years in this House of Commons. He tried to show that in the expenditures of money voted here the Department of Public Works are discriminating against certain provinces. I give him my word that in the last five years nothing of the sort has taken place. I rely on the reports of my officials in thirteen districts all through the country who advise me on the necessity as to buildings, public works or public facilities such as harbours or breakwaters. Take the expenditure in New Brunswick for public buildings, $13-1.000. But the hon. member says they received $765,000 or thereabouts for harbours and rivers. New Brunswick is another province where the fishermen need our help in providing these facilities. They come under federal jurisdiction and we have to do our best to take care of them. Prince Edward Island is in the same position. If you take Quebec, they have all the Gaspe coast, the bay of Chaleur and the St. Lawrence river, and there is fishing there. We maintain harbours and wharves on the St. Lawrence. Why? Because people need those facilities to earn their living, and that is one way to help the public. If you come into Ontario and look at the amount we spend there, it is principally on the great lakes. We have harbours and breakwaters and wharves on the great lakes, which require the expenditure of money. But when I come to Saskatchewan and Alberta I am at a loss to see where I can build wharves or breakwaters or even do dredging. As regards British Columbia, there again they have a long coast. You may say we are spending over $2,000,000 there-
Not nearly enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Perhaps we are not spending enough, but still we are trying to meet the needs of these people on the west coast. They also carry on fishing out there; they have small inlets and harbours, and they have not the means to put up these wharves themselves. I have spoken of harbours and rivers. If you take public buildings, I do not think in the last four years any province has received very much in the way of buildings. If you study my estimates well you will find that in nearly every case the items are revotes because the money could not be spent. I explained that this afternoon at some length. I gave the reasons why we could not proceed; lack of our own staff, lack of building materials, in many instance lack of man-power, and so on. After a survey of the whole country, I wss advised on good

Supply-Public Works
authority, not only by my friends but by people I met throughout the country, that this was not the time to start on a building programme if we wanted to devote most of our energies to putting up homes and taking care of the housing situation. Perhaps we are wrong; perhaps we should drop the housing problem and put up big public buildings in various cities throughout the country. No doubt they are needed', but I am sure the hon. member would be the first to blame me if I did that.

I offered no criticism of the votes for Ottawa, 280, 281 and 282, which total some $13,000,000 and include maintenance and so on. As far as Ontario is concerned, the $2,574,000 includes almost $700,000 to be spent in Ottawa, but the remaining $2,000,000 is to be spent in the west of the province. I quoted these headings separately, in order to distinguish between public buildings and rivers and wharves, or whatever the items cover. I submit that there is an apparent discrimination between Ontario and Quebec on the one hand and the other provinces on the other, and that is the point I had in mind.

I agree with the minister that many matters usually brought up on thg general item could be dealt with very well on specific items as we come to them, but I should like to put on record at least one point. Many acres of land along the shoreline of lake Ontario are being lapped up, and have been lapped up during the past few years, by that lake. If I can be assured by the minister that his department is giving this question serious consideration I do not think any lengthy debate will be necessary.
Mr.FOURNIER (Hull): If the hon. gentleman would wait there is an item under which that question can be discussed. It is item 328, to provide for remedial works where damages are caused by or endanger navigation or federal government structures.
That is all I want to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: That would be the proper item.

I was glad to hear the minister say he had made a tour across the country inquiring into the matters coming under his department. Some years ago, in the days of one of Canada's greatest statesmen, than whom there was no greater, Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made a tour of the west, on which he was accompanied by a predecessor of the minister, Hon. William

Pugsley. An investigation into the problems concerning the navigation of the Saskatchewan river was carried on by the department engineers, whose names I have forgotten for the moment, since I had not intended to say anything about this matter, and they made a report which, I am sure, is available in the department, a copy of which I have in my room. At that time Sir Wilfrid, in addressing a great meeting at St. Andrew's locks, told his listeners what he hoped would follow from the works at St. Andrew's locks was the canalization of the Saskatchewan river right up to Edmonton. I shall not detain the committee longer than to say that since the minister is interested, as I believe he is. and since he has an inquiring mind, I am going to ask him to read the reports which his officials will find for him in the department, and on which Sir Wilfrid based his intention of canalizing that river. Had he lived and been in power to carry out his intention, there would have been harbours and government installations on the Saskatchewan river. The successor to Mr. Pugsley did start some work at Cole rapids, west of the forks of the Saskatchewan, where they remain to this day. I would suggest that when the minister next goes to Prince Albert, I know the city engineer will be glad to drive him down to Cole rapids, as he very kindly drove me there, where he will see the remains of the locks started at that time, still in good condition.
If the hon. gentleman remains as minister I would suggest that later on he bring in a programme for the canalization of the Saskatchewan river as far as Edmonton. This would be a great boon for the west. They would be able to bring low priced but good coal from Edmonton right down to Winnipeg; it would float all the way down to lake Winnipeg. I have been over the course from one end to the other and intended to speak on the matter on another occasion much more fully. This evening, however, I merely wish to invite the minister to follow the footsteps of those other great ministers of public works, Hon. Robert Rogers, who built the locks at Cole rapids, and Hon. William Pugsley, who envisaged them, and planned to canalize the Saskatchewan river. Then, if the minister remains in office long enough to complete a shipping route from Edmonton right down to Winnipeg, hon. gentlemen to my left will not be able on another occasion to charge him with not having canals and locks and harbours in the west to vote money for.

I have endeavoured to be an appreciative audience while hon, members from the prairies have solicited well merited
Supply-Public Works

assistance in order to carry on their industry. I think their demands were justified, and I believe the government have been very generous in making available the millions of dollars they have required to carry on under profitable conditions. However I get a little provoked when we are talking about harbours, breakwaters and dredging to find these members, who have been accorded, generous assistance, taking issue when we of the maritime provinces are undertaking to establish harbour facilities through which they of the western provinces may export their grain to foreign markets. I find it annoying when hon. members from the west take that stand. I believe the Department of Public Works has been fairly generous in affording the maritime provinces facilities required to carry on our fisheries and to provide harbours in order that those in the -west may have an exit to outside markets. Speaking particularly for my own constituency, one which is sea-bound, I would say to the department that there are many things we require. But, speaking generally and without going into detail, I would say that the Department of Public Works has been reasonably generous in affording facilities.
I had not intended speaking at this time, but had decided to wait until later to ask more detailed questions. However I am provoked when I hear western members speak as I have heard them tonight when, as I have said before, we of the east have formed an appreciative audience in respect of the solicitations they have advanced from time to time. I believe it was recognized on both sides of the house that they were justified in what they asked, but I cannot understand any member from the prairies taking issue with the few little incidental items afforded us in the maritime provinces, especially when we have never raised our voices in an antagonistic fashion when they have made requests on behalf of their constituents.

Over a year ago a certain company in Vancouver made an offer to the minister to remove Ripple Rock on a no-cure, no-pay basis. Will the minister make a statement with respect to the action his department has taken on that offer?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I suppose that
in the general discussion I am bound to have something to say about Ripple Rock.
You must have been expecting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Yes, I expected it.
It is your problem child.
Tell them the story about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I think I should. In April, 1942, authority of council was secured to accept the offer of the British Columbia Bridge and Dredging Company Limited to carry out the work of removing Ripple Rock on a cost plus, variable fee basis, the estimated cost supplied by the company at the time being $322,340. The depth to be left after dredging was thirty feet below low water level. The work included the construction of a rock filled dam across the adjacent passage between Maude island and Quadra island, which portion of the work was satisfactorily completed.
The drill barge for the work was designed, tested in model form, and construction put underway.
In the meantime, in October, 1942, inquiry was made on behalf of the United States as to the additional cost of increasing the grade depth to be left after dredging, the additional depth being 3-8 feet. It was during the war that these things took place. The contractors supplied this with their estimate of the cost, including the completed rock dam across Maude island passage, of $473,894, in addition to a fee of $35,000. This was approved by P.C. 2609 of April 1, 1943. The contractors estimated the time required at fifteen months. The barge was outfitted and brought to the site in May, 1943, and moored by cables from the barge winches to heavy concrete anchors dropped in deep water, but it was not until the 15th July that drilling of the rock from the barge commenced.
In October, 1943, it was decided to discontinue operations as the original method appeared to be a failure. Further studies of the problem were made and various discussions were held on the subject by the Canadian and United States authorities.
In October, 1944, authority of council was obtained to accept an offer from the British Columbia Bridge and Dredging Company to make a test for removal of the rock by means of two overhead lines. The test was put under way, but the cost was greater than anticipated and operations were discontinued for a time. The trial was resumed, however, in August, 1945, and continued until the end of September, 1945, at which time the work was suspended as the drill barge required repairs and as unfavourable tidal conditions for further work would ensue for some months.
The contractors were requested to furnish an estimate of cost for completing operations, which they gave at $750,000 with a time for completion of twenty-two months.

Supply-Public Works
As a result of the test referred to above which was carried through to September 29, 1945, some 139 holes had been drilled for a combined length of 714-1 feet, of which ninety-three holes of a combined length of 529 feet had been successfully blasted. The length of the individual hole which can be drilled-that is, between five and six feet- indicates that the problems of removing the rock which had been blasted and of drilling and blasting further holes in order to reach the necessary final agreed depths still remain to be solved.
The contractors were asked to name the sum within which they would guarantee complete removal of the rock to the desired grade. Although in their reply they stated "we are definitely of the opinion that the test as carried out has proven entirely successful and we are convinced that the work should be further proceeded with", they would not give any such guarantee.
The contractors were asked to reconsider their previous estimate of $750,000 and to say if they would undertake to complete the work on a basis of such revised estimate, the performance to be guaranteed by a satisfactory bond under which any cost in excess of the estimate would be shared fifty-fifty by the bonding company and the government. They furnished a revised estimate in the amount of $1.844,428.00, plus a fee of $90,000 and stated that, having approached several reliable bonding companies, they were advised that the bonding companies were not interestedi in writing such a bond. One company agreed to supply a completion bond for any amount, provided that the government would make the necessary payment in cash to be held as security, such security to be the total amount of the bond desired, with the contract to be continued on a cost plus, fixed fee basis.
This department felt hat in the light of three years experience in operating on the project, the contractors should, if they were as confident as they expressed themselves to be that the work could be completed by the methods they proposed, be prepared to submit a firm offer, and. that the suggestion that the excess cost, be shared fifty-fifty was as fair and reasonable as possible under the circumstances.
The whole situation was placed before the committee of the war cabinet. This information was contained in a report we were making to the Department of External Affairs with respect to the whole matter. It was decided at the time that we would, discontinue action until further developments in research in connection with the employment of new enegry methods were made.
When I was out on the coast last fall I do not know how many people called to see me concerning the removal of Ripple Rock. With what they published in the press they nearly had me having bad dreams when I was travelling by boat from Vancouver to Prince Rupert. I speak from memory, but I think the article was headed1, "Sleep well, Mr. Fournier." I passed1 by Ripple Rock about three in the morning, and perhaps they did not think to wake me so I could look at it.
1 spoke to the people there but no one would make a firm bid. I have not the file here but, after I came back to Ottawa, some company wrote in stating that they would handle this work on; a no cure, no pay basis. That is a rather general principle on which to base a contract.
It is a rather advantageous one.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
It all depends
upon the definition given to the word "cure". It did not turn out that way. They wanted to undertake the work and we asked them certain questions concerning the organization of their company and the experience they had in this kind of work. We found that they had no experience. I understand that this was a shipping company established some years ago. Even when we made inquiries to them, they took a long time to reply.
It finally came back to the old system of cost plus. I do not think any hon. member who has been out there and knows the situation would advise the government to undertake this work at the present time without being sure that the amount involved was known to the House of Commons. We have spent some $890,000 on the project up to date, and I would feel ill at ease to spend more of the people's money without some assurance that the work could be done.
Four different schemes have been, suggested to blast away the rock and remove it and to date we have tried three of them. One was to anchor a barge from which drilling operations could be carried on, but it was found that even with the heaviest anchors the barge could not be kept in position so that drilling could be carried on. The drills broke after going in a few inches and we had to discontinue that system. Then they spoke of tunneling under the rock, but the geologists advised that that could not be done because of faults in the rock. Another system suggested was to drop a caisson on the rock, empty it and then drill. However we have no guarantee that that can be done. If we cannot keep a barge in position to do the drilling
Supply-Public Works

we are not too sure that we could bring a cement caisson down there and drop it in the exact position where the work could be done.
There was one method which we thought would be successful. That was to string cables from shore to shore to hold a barge in place. That was the last scheme tried and on which we spent the remainder, of the 1890,000, but it met with little success. Holes were drilled and the rock was blasted, but they were unable to remove the blasted rock and it is still there. They could not drill more than five or six feet at a time and we wanted to go down to a depth of 33 feet. That would have taken between five and six operations of blasting and clearing away the debris. Somebody has suggested that an atomic bomb or atomic energy should be employed, but that is at the study stage only.
It is too close to my home.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I understand that this British Columbia dredging company is well known out there. I think if you met the people who undertook this work before they would not speak as they did five years ago. That is the impression I got when I was on the coast. It would take a brave man to undertake this job and say he will do it at such and such a price. In the department we feel that we cannot spend money endlessly on the project without any guarantee that it will be completed successfully.

It would not take many
wrecks to cost as much as doing the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I admit that. Some engineers say that it is not as dangerous as other people think, but I recall that there was a wreck there.
The government lost one of its own ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
It was a Mines and Resources hydrographic survey boat. On the other hand, hundreds of thousands of boats have been travelling past there for years. The department is studying the effect of the changed currents which were brought about through the closing of Canoe Pass, which work was done under the past contract. The changing of these currents and improved aids have assisted navigation to some extent, and we are awaiting the reaction of the navigators before proceeding with any further attempts at removal.
In all, thirteen schemes have been submitted, most of which are modifications of the schemes that were submitted at the time
public tenders were called for the removal of the rock. All these schemes depend upon the use of present forms of energy. It is considered advisable to await any further action pending the development of new forms of energy that are at present in a research stage.

The minister has suggested that perhaps there is not a firm offer and he talks about spending public money. I did not refer to the earlier history of this rock and the attempts to remove it. My question referred only to the Malahat Shipping Company Limited and their offer to remove Ripple Rock on a no-cure, no-pay basis. On October 23, 1946, they wrote to the minister making the following offer:
We, the Malahat Shipping Company (4934) Limited, a registered contracting company under the Companies Act, under provincial charter No. 18982, undertake to remove the surface of the obstruction known as Ripple Rock, situate in Seymour Narrows, Discovery Passage, between Maud island and Vancouver island, B.C., to a depth of 34 feet low water, spring tides, for a distance of 250 feet by 170 feet, to provide all equipment 'and labour for the said operation, guarantee not to obstruct the free passage of vessels using the channel (with the possible exception of a short period of time whilst fitting overhead wire cables), for the sum of one million five hundred thousand dollars (Mr 500,000) on a "no cure, no pay" basis.
I cannot imagine a more definite offer. No offer could more completely relieve the treasury of any expense in the event of failure. The method proposed is slightly different from any previous one used, in that there will be no barge used. It is proposed to use overhead cables to set up a platform over the rock with anchors and steel elevated piers sunk into the rock itself, the drilling to take place from this platform, which would, of course, not be subject to the tidal forces.
How are you going to anchor these steel columns?
I do not need to be helped; thank you very much.
If you were an engineer you would know they would have to anchor them. That is what is wrong with the entire plan.
I am not aware that the hon. member for Vancouver North is an engineering expert as well as an expert in a lot of other matters.

I know something about mining and I know you would have to drill holes. If the hon. member sticks to the legal profession I think he would do a little better.

Supply-Public Works
Apparently the hon. gentleman who is making these gratuitous interruptions is not interested in having Ripple Rock removed.
I am very much interested in something practical.
I would have thought that he would consider it important enough at least to permit this discussion to continue without trying to embarrass someone else.
We are all interested in that, but we are also interested in saving the taxpayers' money.

Again, what a silly
interruption!

A
silly speech.

I have just read out a firm offer to do this work on a basis where the dominion government will not have to pay one cent if the rock is not removed. How that is a needless waste of public money, I do not know. The hon. member very properly says that I am not an engineer. For any engineering statements I must rely on my informants, but I have an ample file with all sorts of information on this matter, and if the hon. member will hold his peace I will try to get over to the minister what I have to say in as short a space of time as possible. I say again that the hon. member does not aid us in trying to have this matter settled .properly by butting in the way he is doing.
I was describing the difference in the proposed method. I am not going into engineering details. The point I am putting forward is that under this proposal the difficulties which were faced previously-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me one question, is this the first letter that was sent to the Department of Public Works? Has he copies of the other letters which the company sent to us?

Certainly. I have, a voluminous file. I have written to the deputy minister on several occasions on this matter and have had replies from him. I was going to refer to some of those communications. I asked the deputy minister, since my assistance had been asked on several occasions, if he would be kind enough to let me know what was holding up the decision on this offer, and on April 9 last he wrote to me, setting out three matters which would have to be dealt with before the offer could be considered. Those three were: (1) that the company's proposals did not include the removal
of rock No. 2; (2) that proof of the company's financial stability would have to be supplied; and (3) proof of their ability to provide experienced personnel conversant with sub-aqueous rock drilling would have to be provided.
I communicated these requirements, which are, I think, quite proper, to the president of the company, and he replied both to myself and, I think, to the minister. An offer was made to guarantee the removal of rock No. 2 for an additional sum of $200,000. This letter I am reading from is from R. G. Lawson, president of the company, dated April 11, 1947, and is addressed to the minister. It gives an assurance that proof of financial stability through a bank would be provided, and the third requirement was some proof that the company had the experienced) personnel necessary to do this work.
I might also mention that the minister said something about the offer on a "no cure, no pay" basis having been withdrawn or that when you came to investigate it, it was not on a "no cure, no pay" basis. But in this letter dated April 11, last, the offer to do the work on a "no cure, no pay" basis is repeated. I will read that paragraph:
If the federal government is prepared to make a tentative offer, conditional on the company producing proof of finances to undertake the purchase of the necessary material and meet any and all other expenses incurred, vve are prepared to uphold our offer on a "no cure, no pay" basis.
Would the hon. member be kind enough to read that again, as I did not hear it.
I am very sorry I shall not be able to comply with the hon. member's request. He can read it in Hansard tomorrow.
I should like to know it now.

I have in my hand the latest letter I have had from this company, dated June 17 last. As the minister knows, this scheme has been given the blessing of Colonel W. G. Swan, who is a very well known engineer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Have you that in writing?
I have a newspaper clipping to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I should like to see the certificate of engineer Swan on what he advised.

If the minister will let me finish-
Newfoundland

The minister will get it in the morning.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

Monday, June 23, 1947
